title: Plea bargaining (asymmetric information)
text:
Canonical setup (two types)
Defendant type \(\theta\in\{L,H\}\) with prior \(\Pr(H)=\pi\). Type affects conviction probability: \(0<p_L<p_H<1\).
Trial sentence if convicted: \(T>0\).
Plea offer: \(x\).
Trial costs: prosecutor \(c_P>0\), defendant \(c_D>0\).
Defendant accepts iff: \[
x \le p_\theta T + c_D.
\]

title: Plea bargaining (asymmetric information)
text:
Screening pattern (one offer)
To induce \(H\) accept and \(L\) reject: \[
x \in (p_L T + c_D,\; p_H T + c_D].
\]
Expected payoff to prosecutor under this policy: - Type \(H\): \(x\) - Type \(L\) (trial): \(p_L T - c_P\)
So: \[
\pi x + (1-\pi)(p_L T - c_P).
\]

title: Plea bargaining (asymmetric information)
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

Higher \(c_D\) increases plea acceptance.
Higher \(c_P\) increases reliance on pleas.
Stronger evidence (higher \(p_\theta\)) increases acceptance.

title: Life-course dynamics (onset and desistance)
text:
Mechanism (core idea)
Life-course criminology emphasizes that offending is dynamic: - people’s constraints, opportunities, and social ties evolve; - past behavior can affect future options (e.g., stigma, skill loss); - interventions can have different short-run vs long-run effects.
A theory-first approach treats these as state variables.

title: Life-course dynamics (onset and desistance)
text:
Canonical modeling primitives

A) States and transitions
Let state \(x_t\) capture employability, social ties, addiction, stigma, etc. Choices (crime vs no crime) affect: - immediate payoff, - transition of \(x_{t+1}\).


B) Dynamic incentives

“crime today” may increase short-run payoff but worsen future states (stigma, incarceration).
“no crime” may build human capital or relationships, improving future payoffs.



C) Heterogeneity
Different types (impulsive vs patient; high-skill vs low-skill) create persistence and concentration.

title: Life-course dynamics (onset and desistance)
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

Policies that raise short-run costs (sanctions) can deter some behavior but may increase long-run crime if they worsen future states (e.g., incarceration reduces future legal options).
Interventions that improve transitions (training, reentry support) can shift long-run equilibria even if short-run deterrence is unchanged.
Stigma channels can create “path dependence”: early system contact changes the trajectory.

title: Life-course dynamics (onset and desistance)

Evidence often aims to distinguish: - selection (who gets system contact) vs causal impact (contact changes the person), - short-run incapacitation vs long-run dynamic effects.

title: Inequality, deprivation & social trust
text:
Mechanism (core idea)
This mechanism family links macro social conditions to micro behavior through: - outside options (returns to legal work vs illegal gain), - social trust / social capital (willingness to cooperate and enforce norms), - collective efficacy (informal guardianship and community capacity), - stress/strain (pressure and constraints that affect choices).
In theory-first notes, it’s useful to treat inequality/deprivation not as a single cause but as a bundle of parameter shifts affecting incentives and cooperation.

title: Inequality, deprivation & social trust
text:
Canonical modeling primitives

A) Opportunity cost and outside options

legal income option \(w\) vs illegal gain \(b\)
unemployment or low wages reduce \(w\), raising relative attractiveness of crime



B) Trust and collective action

community cooperation increases detection probability \(q\) (through reporting/witnessing)
social capital reduces coordination costs of informal prevention



C) Equilibrium feedback

low trust reduces reporting → lower detection → higher crime → further erosion of trust This can generate multiple equilibria (high-trust/low-crime vs low-trust/high-crime).

title: Inequality, deprivation & social trust
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

Lower outside options (\(w\) down) increase participation in illegal activity when deterrence is unchanged.
Lower trust reduces cooperation and reporting, potentially lowering recorded crime in the short run but raising incidence in the long run.
If trust enters detection, policies that improve legitimacy can shift the system to a different equilibrium.

title: Incentives & deterrence
text:
Mechanism (core idea)
Potential offenders compare expected benefits of offending with expected costs: - probability of detection, - severity of sanction, - opportunity costs (legal work, stigma, future).
In academic work this is often called rational choice or deterrence logic. It does not imply perfect rationality; it is a modeling language for incentives.

title: Incentives & deterrence
section: Canonical model: a simple inspection game
text:
Canonical model: a simple inspection game

Story
A shop owner chooses how intensively to monitor (e.g., cameras/guards). A potential offender chooses whether to steal.


Players and actions

Offender chooses: Crime (\(C\)) or No crime (\(N\)).
Enforcer chooses: Inspect (\(I\)) or Not inspect (\(\bar I\)).



Payoffs (reduced form)
Let: - offender benefit from crime be \(b>0\) if not caught, - sanction (net cost) be \(s>0\) if caught, - inspection cost be \(k>0\) to the enforcer, - harm from a successful crime be \(h>0\) to the enforcer.
Payoffs: - If offender chooses \(N\): offender gets \(0\); enforcer gets \(0\) (regardless of inspection). - If offender chooses \(C\): - if \(I\): offender is caught → payoff \(-s\); enforcer payoff \(-k\) (prevents harm) - if \(\bar I\): offender succeeds → payoff \(b\); enforcer payoff \(-h\)
So the normal-form game is:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& I & \bar I\\ \hline
C & (-s,\,-k) & (b,\,-h)\\
N & (0,\,0) & (0,\,0)
\end{array}
\]

title: Incentives & deterrence
text:
Solved example (mixed-strategy equilibrium)

Problem
Find the mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium (inspection probability and crime probability).


Solution
Let the enforcer inspect with probability \(q\) and the offender commit crime with probability \(p\).
Step 1 (offender indifference condition).
Offender’s expected payoff from \(C\): \[
\mathbb{E}[u_O(C)] = q(-s) + (1-q)b = b - q(b+s).
\] Offender’s payoff from \(N\) is \(0\).
In a mixed equilibrium where offender randomizes, set: \[
b - q(b+s)=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad q^*=\frac{b}{b+s}.
\]
Step 2 (enforcer indifference condition).
Enforcer’s expected payoff from \(I\): \[
\mathbb{E}[u_E(I)] = p(-k) + (1-p)0 = -pk.
\] From \(\bar I\): \[
\mathbb{E}[u_E(\bar I)] = p(-h) + (1-p)0 = -ph.
\] In a mixed equilibrium where enforcer randomizes, set: \[
-pk = -ph \quad \Rightarrow \quad k=h.
\]
This shows an important fact: with this payoff structure, a true interior mixed equilibrium exists only when \(k=h\). Otherwise, the enforcer has a strict preference: - If \(k<h\): inspection is cheaper than expected harm → enforcer prefers inspect. - If \(k>h\): inspection is too costly → enforcer prefers not inspect.


Interpreting the equilibrium cases

If \(k<h\) (inspection relatively effective/cheap): enforcer chooses \(I\), offender chooses \(N\) if \(-s<0\) (always). Crime is deterred.
If \(k>h\) (inspection expensive/ineffective): enforcer chooses \(\bar I\), offender chooses \(C\) if \(b>0\) (always). Crime occurs.

Takeaway: even in a tiny model, deterrence depends on the enforcement cost–harm tradeoff.

title: Incentives & deterrence
text:
Comparative statics (predictions)

Increasing sanction \(s\) reduces the inspection probability needed to deter crime because \(q^*=\frac{b}{b+s}\) decreases in \(s\).
Increasing benefit \(b\) makes deterrence harder (raises \(q^*\)).
Increasing harm \(h\) makes inspection more attractive; increasing cost \(k\) makes it less attractive.

Reporting & legitimacy: observed crime depends on victim reporting and trust.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
Mechanism (core idea)
Behavioral approaches model departures from fully forward-looking choice: - present bias (overweight immediate payoff), - limited attention to detection risk, - self-control constraints.
This does not replace incentive-based models; it changes how incentives are processed.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
Canonical modeling primitives

A) Present-biased utility
A simple representation: - immediate gain from crime is weighted heavily relative to future costs - sanction \(s\) that arrives later is discounted more than “standard” exponential discounting would imply


B) Attention and perceived risk
Perceived detection probability \(\tilde q\) may differ from objective \(q\) due to salience, experience, and misinformation.


C) Commitment and environment
Guardianship/opportunity changes can serve as “commitment devices” by reducing temptations.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

Increasing sanction severity may have weaker deterrent effects when behavior is present-biased (especially if punishment is delayed or uncertain).
Making detection risk salient and immediate can matter more than increasing severity.
Situational prevention (reducing opportunities) can be effective even without changing preferences.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
What would count as evidence? (conceptual)
Studies often focus on: - timing of consequences (immediate vs delayed), - salience interventions (visibility of police, warnings), - measures of impulsivity/self-control correlated with offending.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
Later-on analysis (model links)

Combine with deterrence: replace \(q\) by perceived \(\tilde q\), or change discounting of \(s\).
Combine with opportunity: changes in environment affect temptation and attention.
Dynamic models: repeated experiences update perceived risk and behavior.

title: Policing
text:
Core research questions

How does police presence/effort change incidence vs recorded outcomes (reporting/recording)?
How should scarce resources be allocated across places and times (hotspots, patrol allocation)?
How does legitimacy affect cooperation (reporting, witnessing), and thereby detection?

title: Policing
text:
Institutional primitives (what to model)

A) Capacity and allocation
Policing is constrained: effort must be allocated across: - locations (hotspots vs non-hotspots), - time (day/night; weekends), - tasks (patrol vs investigation).


B) Information and targeting
Police learn from: - calls for service (endogenous reporting), - observed incidents, - intelligence, - past allocation outcomes.


C) Performance measures and incentives
Observed metrics may include: - recorded crime rates, - arrests/clearance rates, - response times, - complaints.
These metrics can shape agency behavior (sometimes away from welfare-maximizing choices).

title: Policing
text:
Strategic responses (equilibrium thinking)

Offender adaptation
Policies can trigger substitution: - location displacement, - temporal displacement, - target substitution, - tactic substitution.


Community cooperation
Reporting and witness cooperation are endogenous and depend on: - expected responsiveness, - perceived fairness, - fear of retaliation, - legitimacy.

title: Stylized facts
text:
This page lists stylized facts: recurring empirical regularities widely discussed in criminology and related social-science literatures.
They are not meant as a complete empirical review, but as constraints for theory: mechanisms and models should be able to reproduce (at least qualitatively) these patterns.
A recurring caution: many “crime facts” depend on measurement (reporting, enforcement, recording practices). When relevant, the fact is stated as a pattern about recorded crime, victimization, or behavior.

title: Stylized facts
text:
1) Concentration in people and places

A small share of people account for a large share of offending (repeat offending / persistence).
Theory implication: heterogeneity and dynamics (states, types, or learning) matter.
Crime concentrates spatially (hotspots: small areas produce disproportionate incidents).
Theory implication: opportunity and guardianship are place-specific; equilibrium responses can relocate activity.

title: Stylized facts
section: 2) Recorded crime is not the same as incidence
text:
2) Recorded crime is not the same as incidence

Not all victimization is reported, and reporting varies by offense type, victim characteristics, and trust in institutions.
Theory implication: include a reporting stage; observed data may reflect participation constraints.
Enforcement is selective: arrest/case data reflect policing choices and capacity, not just offending.
Theory implication: strategic interaction can change observables even when underlying behavior changes less.

(Links) - Legitimacy & compliance → notes/mechanisms/legitimacy-compliance.qmd - Reporting & trust model → notes/models/reporting-trust.qmd

title: Stylized facts
text:
3) Opportunity and routine predict timing

Crime risk often shifts with routine activity patterns (crowding, guardianship, mobility, visibility).
Theory implication: “technology of opportunity” matters; policies can change opportunity without changing preferences.

(Links) - Opportunity / routine activity → notes/mechanisms/opportunity-routine.qmd

title: Stylized facts
section: 4) Sanctions: detection vs severity (and strategic adaptation)
text:
4) Sanctions: detection vs severity (and strategic adaptation)

The deterrent effect of punishment is often discussed as depending on both probability of detection and severity of sanction; in practice, offenders may adapt (switch targets, tactics, locations, or timing).
Theory implication: model deterrence as a game (inspection/monitoring) and allow substitution across actions.

title: Stylized facts
text:
5) Social interactions and networks matter

Offending can be socially embedded: co-offending, peer effects, clustering within networks, diffusion of tactics.
Theory implication: strategic complements, learning, and partner choice can generate clustering and persistence.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text: Screening (principal–agent with adverse selection) studies how a principal designs a menu of contracts to induce agents to reveal private information. Mechanism design generalizes this: choose rules to implement outcomes given strategic agents.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text: Screening (principal–agent with adverse selection) studies how a principal designs a menu of contracts to induce agents to reveal private information. Mechanism design generalizes this: choose rules to implement outcomes given strategic agents.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
What’s special

Key constraint: incentive compatibility (each type prefers its intended option).
Participation (individual rationality) often binds for the lowest type.
Design trades off efficiency vs information rents.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
One example (two-type contract menu)
Agent type \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\) (productivity). Principal offers contracts \((w,q)\): wage and required output.
Utility: \(u = w - c(q,\theta)\), where \(c(q,H) < c(q,L)\) (high type has lower cost).
Principal wants higher \(q\) from \(H\) but must prevent \(H\) from pretending to be \(L\).
Solution sketch. The optimal menu typically: - distorts the low-type contract downward (lower \(q\)) to reduce information rents, - gives the high type a contract with higher \(q\) and positive rent, - satisfies IC constraints: \(H\) prefers \(H\)-contract; \(L\) prefers \(L\)-contract.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
Story
An insurer can’t observe customer risk. It offers two plans (a menu). Customers self-select. The insurer designs the menu so each type reveals itself by choosing the plan intended for it.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
Model

Types \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\) privately known
Contracts \((p,q)\): premium \(p\) and coverage \(q\)
Utility: \(u_\theta(p,q)=v_\theta(q)-p\)
Goal: maximize profit subject to incentive constraints

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
Equilibrium constraints (IC/IR)
Incentive compatibility: \[
u_H(p_H,q_H)\ge u_H(p_L,q_L),
\qquad
u_L(p_L,q_L)\ge u_L(p_H,q_H).
\]
Individual rationality: \[
u_\theta(p_\theta,q_\theta)\ge 0 \quad (\theta\in\{H,L\}).
\]

title: Screening & mechanism design
section: What the solution typically looks like (high-level)
text:
What the solution typically looks like (high-level)

Low-type contract is often distorted (less generous) to reduce information rents.
High type receives more generous terms and may earn positive information rent.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
Later-on analysis

Moral hazard: if effort is hidden too, the design problem changes (adverse selection + moral hazard).
Multiple dimensions: risk + risk aversion produces richer menus.
Mechanism design view: “contract menus” are a specific mechanism; the general theory asks what outcomes are implementable.

title: Cheap talk
text: Cheap talk is communication that is costless and non-binding: a sender sends a message, then a receiver chooses an action.

title: Cheap talk
text: Cheap talk is communication that is costless and non-binding: a sender sends a message, then a receiver chooses an action.

title: Cheap talk
text:
What’s special

Messages have no direct payoff effect, so credibility comes only from aligned incentives.
Information can still be partially transmitted when preferences are not too misaligned.
Outcomes typically depend on how strongly the sender wants to bias the receiver’s action.

title: Cheap talk
text:
One example

Setup (a stylized version)

State: \(\theta \in [0,1]\) is known to the sender.
Message: \(m\) is any costless statement.
Receiver chooses action \(a\in[0,1]\).

Payoffs: - Receiver wants \(a\) close to \(\theta\). - Sender wants \(a\) close to \(\theta + b\) (bias \(b>0\)).


Key idea
If the bias \(b\) is small, the sender can truthfully separate states into intervals (“coarse truth”), and the receiver best-responds by choosing the expected state within the reported interval. If \(b\) is large, communication becomes uninformative (pooling).

title: Cheap talk
text:
Story
You ask a friend for a restaurant recommendation in a new city. Your friend knows the options. But your tastes differ: they love loud, spicy places; you want calm and mild. They aren’t lying—they just have a bias.
Cheap talk studies whether costless messages can still transmit information when incentives aren’t perfectly aligned.

title: Cheap talk
text:
Model

State \(\theta\) known to sender
Message \(m\) is costless and non-binding
Receiver chooses action \(a\)
Preferences are biased

title: Cheap talk
text:
Core math (quadratic loss, bias)
Let \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \(a\in[0,1]\).
Receiver: \[
u_R=-(a-\theta)^2
\]
Sender (bias \(b>0\)): \[
u_S=-(a-(\theta+b))^2
\]

title: Cheap talk
text:
Equilibrium (what to expect)

There is always a babbling equilibrium: messages convey no information and the receiver chooses a constant action (based on the prior).
When bias is not too large, there are partition equilibria: the sender truthfully reveals which interval \(\theta\) lies in; the receiver responds with the conditional mean of that interval.

title: Cheap talk
text:
Later-on analysis

More alignment → more information: smaller bias typically supports finer partitions.
Credibility via commitment: if the sender could commit to a rule (information design), outcomes change drastically.
Costly messages → signaling: adding costs turns cheap talk into signaling.

title: Signaling games
text: A signaling game is a dynamic game with private information: a sender knows their type, chooses a signal (often costly), then a receiver responds.

title: Signaling games
text: A signaling game is a dynamic game with private information: a sender knows their type, chooses a signal (often costly), then a receiver responds.

title: Signaling games
text:
What’s special

Signals can be credible when different types face different costs/benefits (incentive compatibility).
Typical outcomes: separating (types choose different signals), pooling (same signal), or semi-separating.
Beliefs and off-path beliefs matter (PBE / sequential equilibrium ideas).

title: Signaling games
text:
One example (education as a signal)
Types: high ability \(H\) and low ability \(L\).
Sender chooses education level \(e\ge 0\); receiver (employer) offers wage \(w(e)\).

Education is more costly for \(L\) than \(H\) (single-crossing idea): \[
c_L(e) > c_H(e)\ \text{for } e>0.
\]
Employer wants to pay higher wages if they believe the worker is \(H\).

A separating equilibrium can exist where \(H\) chooses a higher \(e\) and \(L\) chooses a lower \(e\), because mimicking is too costly for \(L\). The signal works because it changes beliefs and is differentially costly.

title: Signaling games
text:
Story
A scholarship committee can’t observe applicant ability directly. Applicants can choose to take a difficult certification exam. High-ability students find it less costly; low-ability students find it very costly. The committee conditions its funding decision on the signal.

title: Signaling games
text:
Model

Types: \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\), prior \(p\)
Signal: \(e\in\{0,1\}\) with costs \(c_H(1)<c_L(1)\) and \(c_H(0)=c_L(0)=0\)
Receiver chooses reward based on beliefs after observing \(e\)

title: Signaling games
text:
Equilibrium (separating vs pooling)
Let the reward be \(w_H\) if perceived high type and \(w_L\) otherwise.
A separating equilibrium with \(H\) choosing \(e=1\) and \(L\) choosing \(e=0\) requires: \[
w_H-c_H(1)\ge w_L
\quad\text{and}\quad
w_H-c_L(1)\le w_L.
\]

title: Signaling games
text:
Later-on analysis

Pooling: if costs aren’t different enough, both types choose the same signal (signal loses meaning).
Off-path beliefs: dynamic equilibrium concepts differ in how they restrict beliefs after unexpected signals.
Continuous effort: allowing \(e\) continuous yields richer separating thresholds and comparative statics.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text: Evolutionary game theory studies strategy change over time via selection, imitation, or learning. Instead of fully rational choice each period, strategy shares evolve.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text: Evolutionary game theory studies strategy change over time via selection, imitation, or learning. Instead of fully rational choice each period, strategy shares evolve.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
What’s special

Focus shifts from equilibrium as a static concept to stability under dynamics.
Key objects: ESS (evolutionarily stable strategy), replicator dynamics, learning rules.
Useful when players are boundedly rational or populations adapt.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
One example (replicator dynamics, 2 strategies)
Let the population share using strategy 1 be \(x\in[0,1]\). If payoffs are \(\pi_1(x)\) and \(\pi_2(x)\), replicator dynamics are:
\[
\dot{x} = x(1-x)\bigl(\pi_1(x)-\pi_2(x)\bigr).
\]
Intuition: the share of a strategy grows when it performs better than the alternative. Fixed points correspond to states where neither strategy has a payoff advantage.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Story
In a large community, newcomers copy behaviors that seem to “work.” Strategies that perform better spread. Nobody solves the game explicitly, yet population patterns evolve.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Model

Strategies are held by a population
Relative payoff determines growth
Dynamics describe how shares change

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Dynamics (replicator)
Let \(x\) be the share playing strategy 1, payoffs \(\pi_1(x)\) and \(\pi_2(x)\): \[
\dot{x}=x(1-x)\bigl(\pi_1(x)-\pi_2(x)\bigr).
\]

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Equilibrium / stability (what to look for)

Rest points satisfy \(\dot{x}=0\) (often \(x=0\), \(x=1\), or where \(\pi_1(x)=\pi_2(x)\)).
Stability depends on whether nearby deviations push \(x\) back or away.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Later-on analysis

ESS: a refinement capturing robustness to mutant invasions.
Learning rules: fictitious play, reinforcement learning, best-response dynamics.
Link to Nash: some dynamics converge to Nash in certain classes of games, but not always.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text: Global games study equilibrium selection in coordination games by adding small private noise to information about fundamentals.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text: Global games study equilibrium selection in coordination games by adding small private noise to information about fundamentals.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
What’s special

Many coordination games have multiple equilibria (good/bad outcomes).
Tiny informational frictions can select a unique equilibrium.
Provides a disciplined way to talk about “which equilibrium happens” without arbitrary refinements.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
One example (currency-attack intuition)
A government defends a peg if fundamentals are strong; speculators attack if they expect others to attack.
Each speculator observes a noisy signal of the fundamental. If signals are slightly noisy, an equilibrium often takes a threshold form: attack if your signal is below a cutoff. The cutoff is pinned down endogenously, yielding a unique prediction.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Story
A bank can survive if depositors stay calm, but fails if too many withdraw. Everyone hears rumors, each slightly noisy. If you expect others to run, running is rational; if you expect calm, staying is rational. Multiple equilibria appear.
Global games add tiny private noise and often recover a single “threshold” prediction.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Model

Fundamental \(\theta\) (bank strength)
Private signal: \(x_i=\theta+\varepsilon_i\)
Action: withdraw or stay
Payoffs depend on the fraction withdrawing

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Equilibrium (threshold form, idea)
A typical global-games prediction is: - withdraw iff \(x_i \le x^*\)
The cutoff \(x^*\) solves an indifference condition at which a depositor is just willing to withdraw.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Later-on analysis

Selection: small noise breaks multiplicity and selects one equilibrium.
Policy: transparency and information disclosure can move the cutoff.
Related models: currency attacks, coordination failures, debt rollovers.

title: Extensive-form games
text: An extensive-form game represents timing (who moves when) and information (what players observe) using a game tree.

title: Extensive-form games
text: An extensive-form game represents timing (who moves when) and information (what players observe) using a game tree.

title: Extensive-form games
text:
What’s special

Sequential rationality matters: players optimize at every decision node.
The standard solution is subgame perfect equilibrium via backward induction (perfect information case).

title: Extensive-form games
text:
One example (backward induction)





flowchart TD
  S((Start)) -->|P1: A| A(( ))
  S -->|P1: B| B(( ))
  A -->|P2: L| AL["(2,1)"]
  A -->|P2: R| AR["(0,0)"]
  B -->|P2: L| BL["(1,2)"]
  B -->|P2: R| BR["(3,0)"]






Player 2 chooses L after \(A\) (since \(1>0\)) and L after \(B\) (since \(2>0\)).
Anticipating this, player 1 prefers \(A\) (since \(2>1\)). Outcome: \((A,L)\).

title: Extensive-form games
text:
Story
A landlord, Ms. K, is renewing a lease with Rin. The neighborhood has improved, and Ms. K considers raising rent. Ms. K chooses first: a moderate raise or an aggressive one. Rin then decides: accept or move out.
The key is timing: Rin observes the offer before acting, and Ms. K anticipates Rin’s response.

title: Extensive-form games
text:
Model

Player 1 (landlord): \(L\) (low increase) or \(H\) (high increase)
Player 2 (tenant): after observing, \(A\) (accept) or \(M\) (move)
Information: perfect (tenant observes the offer)
Solution concept: backward induction / SPE

title: Extensive-form games
text:
Game tree (toy)





flowchart TD
  S((Start)) -->|P1: L| L(( ))
  S -->|P1: H| H(( ))
  L -->|P2: A| LA["(2,2)"]
  L -->|P2: M| LM["(0,1)"]
  H -->|P2: A| HA["(3,0)"]
  H -->|P2: M| HM["(0,1)"]

title: Extensive-form games
text:
Equilibrium (backward induction → SPE)
Step 1 (tenant’s optimal actions at the second stage): - After \(L\): compare tenant payoff \(2\) (accept) vs \(1\) (move) → choose \(A\) - After \(H\): compare tenant payoff \(0\) (accept) vs \(1\) (move) → choose \(M\)
Step 2 (landlord anticipates this): - If choose \(L\) → outcome \((2,2)\) - If choose \(H\) → tenant moves → outcome \((0,1)\)
So landlord chooses \(L\).
SPE outcome: \((L,A)\).

title: Extensive-form games
text:
Later-on analysis

Outside option changes: if moving becomes less costly, the landlord’s ability to raise rent shrinks.
Incomplete information: if Ms. K doesn’t know Rin’s moving cost, the game becomes Bayesian and can generate screening/signaling behavior.
Commitment: if Rin could commit to “move if any increase,” outcomes shift again (commitment changes the tree).

title: Bargaining
text: Bargaining models how parties negotiate over surplus (price, wage, division of a pie), often with disagreement or delay.

title: Bargaining
text: Bargaining models how parties negotiate over surplus (price, wage, division of a pie), often with disagreement or delay.

title: Bargaining
text:
What’s special

Timing and outside options shape outcomes.
With discounting, delay is costly → early agreement is attractive.
Incomplete information introduces screening and strategic delay.

title: Bargaining
text:
One example (alternating-offers, intuition)
Two players bargain over splitting 1. In each round, one proposes a split; the other accepts or rejects. If rejected, bargaining continues next round with discount factor \(\delta\).
Backward induction in the infinite-horizon model yields immediate agreement: the proposer offers the responder just enough to make them indifferent between accepting now vs rejecting and waiting. More patient players (higher \(\delta\)) obtain better terms.

title: Bargaining
text:
Story
Two coauthors must decide authorship order before tomorrow’s submission deadline. Delay is costly: missing the deadline reduces the paper’s impact. One proposes a split; the other can accept or reject. If rejected, the other proposes next round.

title: Bargaining
text:
Model

Pie size: 1
Alternating offers
Common discount factor: \(\delta\in(0,1)\)
Solution concept: subgame perfect equilibrium

title: Bargaining
text:
Equilibrium (Rubinstein alternating offers, symmetric discounting)
In the infinite-horizon alternating-offers model with the same discount factor \(\delta\) for both players, the unique SPE split is:

First proposer receives: \[
\frac{1}{1+\delta}
\]
Responder receives: \[
\frac{\delta}{1+\delta}.
\]

Intuition: rejecting means you become proposer next round, but you discount the future by \(\delta\).

title: Bargaining
text:
Later-on analysis

Asymmetric patience: if one player has higher \(\delta\), they get a larger share.
Outside options: disagreement payoffs shift the split.
Incomplete information: can generate delay, signaling, and “toughness” reputations.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
A correlated equilibrium (CE) allows players to condition their actions on a shared signal (a recommendation from a mediator). The signal can correlate players’ actions.
A distribution over action profiles is a CE if, when a player receives a recommendation, they have no incentive to deviate given they believe others follow their recommendations.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
A correlated equilibrium (CE) allows players to condition their actions on a shared signal (a recommendation from a mediator). The signal can correlate players’ actions.
A distribution over action profiles is a CE if, when a player receives a recommendation, they have no incentive to deviate given they believe others follow their recommendations.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games
Information and mediation (recommendation systems)
Mechanism design / persuasion / traffic routing interpretations
Computational game theory (CE is often easier to compute than NE)

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Choose a distribution over action profiles (a “correlation device”).
For each player and each recommended action, write the no-deviation (obedience) constraints:

expected payoff from following ≥ expected payoff from deviating.

If all obedience constraints hold, the distribution is a correlated equilibrium.

title: Correlated equilibrium
section: Solved example (a simple CE that improves outcomes)
text:
Solved example (a simple CE that improves outcomes)

Problem (context + question)
Two drivers choose routes: \(A\) or \(B\). If both choose the same route, there is congestion and each gets 0. If they choose different routes, each gets 1.
Payoffs: - If actions differ: payoff 1 each - If same: payoff 0 each
Question: Construct a correlated equilibrium that achieves expected payoff 1 for each driver.


Solution
Consider a mediator who flips a fair coin and privately recommends: - with probability 1/2: recommend (Driver 1: A, Driver 2: B) - with probability 1/2: recommend (Driver 1: B, Driver 2: A)
So the induced distribution puts probability 1/2 on (A,B) and 1/2 on (B,A).
Step 1: Check obedience for Driver 1 - If Driver 1 is told “A”, they infer Driver 2 was told “B”, so following yields payoff 1. Deviating to “B” would match Driver 2 and yield 0. - If Driver 1 is told “B”, symmetric: follow yields 1; deviating yields 0.
So Driver 1 never wants to deviate. Same for Driver 2.
Result: This recommendation device is a correlated equilibrium with payoff 1 for each.


Takeaway
CE allows coordination using signals, often improving welfare relative to uncoordinated play.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
Later-on analysis

Every Nash equilibrium induces a correlated equilibrium (as a special case), but CE can be larger.
CE is closely related to “obedience constraints” in mechanism design.
If you ever do computation: CE can be found via linear programming in finite games.

title: Equilibria
text: Equilibrium cheat sheet

title: Equilibria
text:
Core (most used)

Nash equilibrium (NE)
Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
Sequential equilibrium

title: Equilibria
text:
Refinements (when credibility matters)

Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
Proper equilibrium

title: Equilibria
text:
Alternatives / related notions

Correlated equilibrium
Rationalizability
Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)

title: Rationalizability
text:
Rationalizability predicts which actions can be justified as best responses to some beliefs about others’ actions, assuming everyone is rational and this is common knowledge.
It often corresponds to iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS). (With weak dominance, elimination order can matter, so newcomers usually start with strict dominance.)

title: Rationalizability
text:
Rationalizability predicts which actions can be justified as best responses to some beliefs about others’ actions, assuming everyone is rational and this is common knowledge.
It often corresponds to iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS). (With weak dominance, elimination order can matter, so newcomers usually start with strict dominance.)

title: Rationalizability
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games when you want predictions weaker than Nash
Settings with equilibrium multiplicity (rationalizability gives a set of plausible actions)
As a foundation for epistemic game theory

title: Rationalizability
section: How to solve (recipe: iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies)
text:
How to solve (recipe: iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies)

Identify strictly dominated actions for any player and remove them.
Recompute dominance in the reduced game.
Repeat until no more strictly dominated actions remain.
The remaining actions are rationalizable.

title: Rationalizability
text:
Solved example (iterated deletion)

Problem (context + question)
Player 1 actions: \(U, M, D\). Player 2 actions: \(L, R\). Payoffs to player 1 are:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& L & R\\ \hline
U & 3 & 0\\
M & 2 & 1\\
D & 1 & 0
\end{array}
\]
Assume player 2’s payoffs are irrelevant for this exercise.
Question: Which actions of player 1 are rationalizable by iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies?


Solution
Compare player 1 actions:

Does \(D\) get strictly dominated by \(M\)?

Against \(L\): \(u_1(M)=2 > u_1(D)=1\)
Against \(R\): \(u_1(M)=1 > u_1(D)=0\) Yes: \(M\) strictly dominates \(D\).


So eliminate \(D\).
Now remaining actions for player 1: \(U\) and \(M\). - Does \(U\) strictly dominate \(M\)? No: - Against \(L\): \(U=3 > M=2\) - Against \(R\): \(U=0 < M=1\) - Does \(M\) strictly dominate \(U\)? No, same reason.
Result: The rationalizable actions for player 1 are \(\{U, M\}\).


Takeaway
Rationalizability removes clearly irrational actions but may still leave multiple plausible choices.

title: Rationalizability
text:
Later-on analysis

Nash equilibrium is a stronger prediction than rationalizability.
In some games, iterated strict dominance leads to a unique outcome (then it’s very powerful).
With weak dominance, elimination can depend on order; if you include it, add a warning section.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
A proper equilibrium is a refinement of trembling-hand perfection. It assumes players can make mistakes, but very bad mistakes are much less likely than slightly bad ones.
Intuition: if an action yields a much lower payoff than another, the chance you mistakenly choose it should be much smaller.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
A proper equilibrium is a refinement of trembling-hand perfection. It assumes players can make mistakes, but very bad mistakes are much less likely than slightly bad ones.
Intuition: if an action yields a much lower payoff than another, the chance you mistakenly choose it should be much smaller.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games with multiple perfect equilibria
Equilibrium selection arguments based on “plausible mistakes”
Advanced micro/game theory refinements

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Start from candidate equilibria (usually Nash / perfect).
Compare payoffs of different deviations.
Impose the idea: probability of a worse deviation is tiny relative to a better deviation.
Check whether the equilibrium can be supported as the limit of such “proper” trembles.

(For most newcomer notes, the key is the intuition, not the full formal definition.)

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
Solved example (intuition with unequal mistakes)

Problem (context + question)
Player 1 is choosing between three actions \(A,B,C\) against a fixed opponent strategy. Payoffs to player 1 are:

\(u_1(A)=10\) (best)
\(u_1(B)=9\) (slightly worse)
\(u_1(C)=0\) (much worse)

Question: Under the “proper” idea of trembles, which mistake is more plausible: choosing \(B\) or choosing \(C\)?


Solution
Proper equilibrium assumes that when players tremble: - they might mistakenly choose \(B\) instead of \(A\) with small probability, - but choosing \(C\) (which is drastically worse) should be far less likely than choosing \(B\).
So “proper trembles” treat worse errors as exponentially rarer than mild errors.
Result: A proper refinement would allow small probability on \(B\) but push the probability on \(C\) to be negligible relative to \(B\) as trembles vanish.


Check
This matches the guiding principle: the likelihood of mistakes respects payoff ranking and payoff gaps.


Takeaway
Proper equilibrium captures “bounded rationality with common sense”: huge blunders are rarer than small slips.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
Later-on analysis

Proper equilibrium ⟹ trembling-hand perfect ⟹ Nash (in finite games).
In practice, proper equilibrium is used when you want a sharper selection than perfection provides.
If you later want a fully formal statement, we can add it as an appendix section.

title: Sequential equilibrium
text:
A sequential equilibrium is a refinement of PBE. It is a pair (strategies, beliefs) such that:

Sequential rationality: strategies are optimal at every information set given beliefs.
Consistency: beliefs come from strategies via Bayes’ rule as limits of fully mixed (“trembling”) strategies.

This “tremble” requirement disciplines off-path beliefs: beliefs must be justifiable by small mistakes.

title: Sequential equilibrium
text:
A sequential equilibrium is a refinement of PBE. It is a pair (strategies, beliefs) such that:

Sequential rationality: strategies are optimal at every information set given beliefs.
Consistency: beliefs come from strategies via Bayes’ rule as limits of fully mixed (“trembling”) strategies.

This “tremble” requirement disciplines off-path beliefs: beliefs must be justifiable by small mistakes.

title: Sequential equilibrium
text:
Where it shows up

Signaling games and dynamic games with imperfect information
Any setting where PBE has many equilibria due to arbitrary off-path beliefs
Refinement discussions in micro theory / game theory texts

title: Sequential equilibrium
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Start from a candidate PBE.
Add small probabilities (trembles) so every action is played with positive probability.
Compute beliefs via Bayes’ rule under the perturbed strategy.
Take limits as trembles go to zero:

if beliefs converge, they are consistent.

Check sequential rationality with those beliefs.

title: Sequential equilibrium
section: Solved example (why some off-path beliefs are not credible)
text:
Solved example (why some off-path beliefs are not credible)

Problem (context + question)
Consider the pooling PBE from the PBE page: - Both types choose \(e=0\). - Off-path belief after \(e=1\) is \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)=0\).
Question: Explain the consistency idea: what must be true for such an off-path belief to be allowed under sequential equilibrium?


Solution
Sequential equilibrium requires off-path beliefs to be limits of Bayes-updated beliefs from fully mixed strategies.
So imagine a perturbed (trembling) strategy where: - Type \(H\) plays \(e=1\) with small probability \(\varepsilon_H>0\), - Type \(L\) plays \(e=1\) with small probability \(\varepsilon_L>0\).
Then, upon observing \(e=1\), Bayes’ rule gives: \[
\Pr(H\mid e=1)=\frac{p\,\varepsilon_H}{p\,\varepsilon_H+(1-p)\,\varepsilon_L}.
\]
Now consider the limit as trembles vanish. The limiting belief depends on the relative rate at which \(\varepsilon_H\) and \(\varepsilon_L\) go to zero.

If \(\varepsilon_H/\varepsilon_L \to 0\), then \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)\to 0\).
If \(\varepsilon_H/\varepsilon_L \to \infty\), then \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)\to 1\).
If \(\varepsilon_H/\varepsilon_L \to k\in(0,\infty)\), then the limit is an interior number in \((0,1)\).

Result: The off-path belief \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)=0\) is consistent only if the perturbations imply that, in the limit, type \(H\) is vanishingly less likely than type \(L\) to make that mistake.


Check
This belief is not “free”: it must be explainable by a sequence of fully mixed strategies.


Takeaway
Sequential equilibrium restricts off-path beliefs by requiring them to arise from plausible small mistakes.

title: Sequential equilibrium
text:
Later-on analysis

Sequential equilibrium is often closer to how theorists think about “reasonable beliefs” off-path.
Stronger refinements (e.g., intuitive criterion) impose additional structure.
For applied work, PBE is common; for selection arguments, sequential equilibrium is a useful upgrade.

title: Nash equilibrium (NE)
text:
A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where no player can gain by deviating unilaterally.
In a finite game with strategy sets \(S_i\) and payoffs \(u_i\), a profile \(s^*=(s_1^*,\dots,s_n^*)\) is a Nash equilibrium if for every player \(i\): \[
u_i(s_i^*,s_{-i}^*) \ge u_i(s_i,s_{-i}^*) \quad \forall s_i\in S_i.
\]

title: Nash equilibrium (NE)
text:
A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where no player can gain by deviating unilaterally.
In a finite game with strategy sets \(S_i\) and payoffs \(u_i\), a profile \(s^*=(s_1^*,\dots,s_n^*)\) is a Nash equilibrium if for every player \(i\): \[
u_i(s_i^*,s_{-i}^*) \ge u_i(s_i,s_{-i}^*) \quad \forall s_i\in S_i.
\]

title: Nash equilibrium (NE)
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games (simultaneous move)
Any finite game once written in normal form (including mixed strategies)
As a building block inside more advanced equilibrium concepts

title: Nash equilibrium (NE)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Pure strategies

(Optional) Check for strict dominance and eliminate dominated actions.
Compute each player’s best response to every opponent action.
Nash equilibria are intersections of best responses.



Mixed strategies (2×2 or small games)

Guess supports (which actions get positive probability).
Impose indifference conditions: each player mixes only if the opponent makes them indifferent over actions in support.
Solve probabilities + verify they lie in \([0,1]\) and no excluded action yields higher payoff.

title: Nash equilibrium (NE)
text:
Solved example (pure NE)

Problem (context + question)
Two cafés simultaneously choose discount \(D\) or normal pricing \(N\). Payoffs are:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& D & N\\ \hline
D & (1,1) & (3,0)\\
N & (0,3) & (2,2)
\end{array}
\]
Question: Find all pure-strategy Nash equilibria.


Solution
Step 1 (player 1 best responses): - If player 2 plays \(D\), player 1 compares \(1\) (play \(D\)) vs \(0\) (play \(N\)) → best response is \(D\). - If player 2 plays \(N\), player 1 compares \(3\) (play \(D\)) vs \(2\) (play \(N\)) → best response is \(D\).
So player 1’s best response is always \(D\).
Step 2 (player 2 best responses): By symmetry, player 2’s best response is always \(D\).
Result: The unique pure-strategy Nash equilibrium is \((D,D)\).


Check
At \((D,D)\), deviating to \(N\) reduces each café’s payoff from \(1\) to \(0\).


Takeaway
NE can be inefficient: both cafés would prefer \((N,N)\), but strategic incentives push them to discount.

title: Nash equilibrium (NE)
text:

title: Convexity & concavity
text:
A set \(C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) is convex if for any \(x,y\in C\) and any \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[
\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y \in C.
\]
Intuition. If you can take “mixtures” of two feasible points and stay feasible, the set is convex. This is exactly why mixed strategies live in a simplex.

title: Convexity & concavity
text:
A set \(C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) is convex if for any \(x,y\in C\) and any \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[

\]

title: Convexity & concavity
text:
Concave functions
A function \(f\) is concave on a convex set if for any \(x,y\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[
f(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y)\ge \lambda f(x) + (1-\lambda)f(y).
\]
Intuition. Concavity means “diminishing returns” and makes optimization well-behaved: local maxima are global.

title: Convexity & concavity
section: Example: why concavity helps best responses
text:
Example: why concavity helps best responses
Let \(f(x)=2x-x^2\) on \([0,2]\). Then \(f''(x)=-2<0\), so \(f\) is concave and the maximizer is unique.
FOC: \(f'(x)=2-2x=0 \Rightarrow x^*=1\).
In games, concavity in your own action often implies a unique best response.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
In Bayesian and information economics, “information” is usually represented by what events a player can distinguish.
There are two common (equivalent) ways to think about it:

Information partition (finite case): a player observes which cell of a partition they are in.
\(\sigma\)-algebra (general case): the collection of events the player can condition on.

You almost never need heavy measure theory for standard game theory notes—just the intuition.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
In Bayesian and information economics, “information” is usually represented by what events a player can distinguish.
There are two common (equivalent) ways to think about it:

Information partition (finite case): a player observes which cell of a partition they are in.
\(\sigma\)-algebra (general case): the collection of events the player can condition on.

You almost never need heavy measure theory for standard game theory notes—just the intuition.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
\(\sigma\)-algebra (concept only)
Let \(\Omega\) be the set of possible states of the world.
A \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F}\) is a collection of subsets of \(\Omega\) (events) such that:

\(\Omega \in \mathcal{F}\)

If \(A \in \mathcal{F}\) then \(A^c \in \mathcal{F}\)

If \(A_1, A_2, \dots \in \mathcal{F}\) then \(\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty A_k \in \mathcal{F}\)

Intuition. \(\mathcal{F}\) lists the events you are able to talk about (and condition on).
Coarser \(\mathcal{F}\) = less information.

Finite shortcut (partition view)
If \(\Omega\) is finite and a player’s information is a partition \[
\Pi = \{C_1,\dots,C_m\},
\] then the player can distinguish only which cell \(C_j\) contains the true state.
The corresponding \(\sigma\)-algebra is “all unions of cells of \(\Pi\)”.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
section: Conditional expectation as “best prediction given information”
text:
Conditional expectation as “best prediction given information”
Given an integrable random variable \(X\) (e.g., payoff-relevant quantity) and an information set \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) is the random variable that represents the best mean-squared prediction of \(X\) using only information in \(\mathcal{G}\).
Projection idea (intuition). Think of \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) as projecting \(X\) onto the space of \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable variables (things you can compute using the information you have).

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
section: Example: conditional expectation with a partition
text:
Example: conditional expectation with a partition
Let the state space be \[
\Omega=\{\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4\},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(\omega_k)=\tfrac14 \text{ for each }k.
\]
Let \[
X(\omega_1)=0,\;X(\omega_2)=2,\;X(\omega_3)=4,\;X(\omega_4)=6.
\]
Suppose the player only observes whether the state is in \[
C_1=\{\omega_1,\omega_2\}\quad\text{or}\quad C_2=\{\omega_3,\omega_4\}.
\]
That information corresponds to a partition \(\Pi=\{C_1,C_2\}\) (and a \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by it).
Then the conditional expectation is constant on each cell:

On \(C_1\): \[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid C_1]
=\frac{X(\omega_1)+X(\omega_2)}{2}
=\frac{0+2}{2}=1.
\]
On \(C_2\): \[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid C_2]
=\frac{X(\omega_3)+X(\omega_4)}{2}
=\frac{4+6}{2}=5.
\]

So \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) takes value \(1\) if you learn “cell \(C_1\)”, and value \(5\) if you learn “cell \(C_2\)”.
Game theory interpretation. This is exactly what beliefs do: you map what you observed to an updated expectation of payoff-relevant quantities.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
Common knowledge (concept)
An event \(E\) is common knowledge if: - everyone knows \(E\), - everyone knows that everyone knows \(E\), - everyone knows that everyone knows that everyone knows \(E\), - and so on indefinitely.
Intuition. Common knowledge is what makes coordination possible (or impossible). It is stronger than “everyone knows”.

Iterated beliefs (one-line idea)
In Bayesian games, strategies can depend on: - beliefs about types, - beliefs about others’ beliefs, - higher-order beliefs.
Often you don’t compute these explicitly; you just need to know they exist and that equilibrium concepts impose consistency.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
Practical takeaway
For most game theory work: - partitions are enough to model information, - conditional expectation captures “best prediction given what you know”, - common knowledge / higher-order beliefs matter conceptually for coordination and equilibrium.

title: Linear algebra
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability vector over pure actions. If player \(i\) has \(m\) pure actions, a mixed strategy is
\[
\Delta^{m-1}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^m:\; x_k\ge 0\;\forall k,\;\sum_{k=1}^m x_k = 1\right\},
\]
the \((m-1)\)-simplex.
Intuition. You can think of \(x\) as a “weighting” of actions. The simplex condition just says: nonnegative weights that sum to 1.

title: Linear algebra
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability vector over pure actions. If player \(i\) has \(m\) pure actions, a mixed strategy is
\[
\Delta^{m-1}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^m:\; x_k\ge 0\;\forall k,\;\sum_{k=1}^m x_k = 1\right\},
\]
the \((m-1)\)-simplex.
Intuition. You can think of \(x\) as a “weighting” of actions. The simplex condition just says: nonnegative weights that sum to 1.

title: Linear algebra
text:
Payoff matrices and expected payoff
In a two-player normal-form game, let player 1 have \(m\) actions and player 2 have \(n\) actions. Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be player 1’s payoff matrix (and \(B\) for player 2). If player 1 plays \(x\in\Delta^{m-1}\) and player 2 plays \(y\in\Delta^{n-1}\), then player 1’s expected payoff is
\[
u_1(x,y)=x^\top A y.
\]
Intuition. First compute expected payoffs against each of player 2’s pure actions (\(Ay\)). Then average those numbers using player 1’s mixing weights (\(x^\top\)).

title: Linear algebra
text:
Example: 2×2 game
Suppose
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 0\\
1 & 3
\end{pmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{pmatrix}0.4\\0.6\end{pmatrix},\quad
y=\begin{pmatrix}0.25\\0.75\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Compute
\[
Ay=
\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 0\\
1 & 3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
0.25\\0.75
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.5\\
2.5
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
u_1(x,y)=x^\top(Ay)=0.4\cdot 0.5+0.6\cdot 2.5=1.7.
\]
So the mixed-vs-mixed expected payoff is \(1.7\) for player 1.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
This page collects non-clinical, skills-based tools that reliably change behavior through mechanisms you’ve already covered: attention, learning, emotion regulation, and environment design.
It is not therapy advice or diagnosis. It’s a toolkit of methods that show up in many evidence-based approaches.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
Tool 1: Implementation intentions (if–then plans)
Format: - “If situation S happens, then I will do action A.”
Why it works: - links cues to desired actions, - reduces working-memory demand at the moment of choice.
Prediction pattern: works best when S is specific and A is small and feasible.

title: Tools for behavior change
section: Tool 2: Behavioral activation (do first, feel later)
text:
Tool 2: Behavioral activation (do first, feel later)
When mood is low, waiting for motivation often fails. Behavioral activation: - schedules small rewarding/meaningful actions, - rebuilds reinforcement and routine.
Mechanism: learning + reward + breaking withdrawal loops.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
Tool 3: Reappraisal (change the interpretation)
Reappraisal changes how an event is construed: - from insult → misunderstanding, - from catastrophe → challenge, - from personal failure → information.
Mechanism: emotion regulation via appraisal shifts.
Prediction pattern: reappraisal is easier before arousal peaks.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
Tool 4: Exposure (reduce avoidance loops)
Avoidance reduces anxiety short-run but maintains it long-run. Exposure: - safely faces the cue in graded steps, - allows prediction errors (“I can tolerate this”).
Mechanism: learning under uncertainty; updating threat associations.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
Tool 5: Friction and defaults (environment design)
If a behavior is cue-driven, modify the environment: - add friction to harmful routines, - make desired routines the default.
Mechanism: attention + habit control.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
Tool 6: Values and identity alignment
Change sticks when behavior is identity-consistent: - “I’m the kind of person who…” - tie actions to meaning rather than only outcomes.
Mechanism: motivation + norms + self-concept.

title: Tools for behavior change
section: Tool 7: Repair scripts (for relationships and institutions)
text:
Tool 7: Repair scripts (for relationships and institutions)
Repair is structured: - acknowledge → validate → explain → commit → compensate (when appropriate)
Mechanism: reduces threat, restores trust, resets norms.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
A reusable behavior-change plan template

Identify the cue (when/where/with whom)

Identify the loop (urge → action → reward/relief)

Pick one lever: cues, friction, substitute routine, reappraisal, exposure, support

Define one measurable micro-action

Add feedback: tracking, accountability, or public commitment

Plan for slips: “slip ≠ collapse” script

title: Moral psychology
text:
Moral psychology studies how people judge right and wrong, and why they enforce norms. It connects directly to: - punishment and forgiveness, - legitimacy and compliance, - polarization and “moralized” conflict.
This page uses a mechanism-first approach: moral intuitions + emotion + identity → judgments and enforcement.

title: Moral psychology
text:
Two systems (a useful simplification)
Moral judgment often reflects interaction between: - fast intuitions (emotion and gut reactions), - slower reasoning (justification, consistency checks).
Reasoning is important, but often functions as: - clarification and coherence, - persuasion, - post-hoc explanation.
Pitfall: assuming that moral disagreement is mostly about facts. Often it’s about values, identity, and perceived intent.

title: Moral psychology
text:
Key objects in moral cognition

Harm and care
People react strongly to perceived harm, especially intentional harm.
Prediction pattern: perceived intentionality increases blame and punishment.


Fairness and reciprocity
Unfairness triggers anger and punitive motivation. Reciprocity supports cooperation.
Prediction pattern: people punish unfairness even when punishment is costly.


Loyalty and group-boundaries
Group membership shapes whose suffering is salient and whose claims are credible.
Prediction pattern: moral judgments become harsher when out-groups are seen as threatening or disrespectful.


Authority and legitimacy
People often treat legitimate authority as morally relevant: - “rules exist for a reason” - “respect the process”
Prediction pattern: procedural fairness increases voluntary compliance.


Purity and contamination (where relevant)
Some moral judgments are linked to disgust and boundary maintenance.
Prediction pattern: disgust can increase harshness even when harm is unclear.

title: Moral psychology
section: Emotion as the engine of moral enforcement
text:
Emotion as the engine of moral enforcement
Moral emotions drive action: - anger → punishment and confrontation - disgust → exclusion and distancing - shame → concealment and conformity pressure - guilt → repair and apology - contempt → status downgrading and dehumanization risk
Prediction pattern: when anger is high, people over-attribute intentionality and demand harsher sanctions.

title: Moral psychology
text:
Intentions matter (often more than outcomes)
People judge harm differently based on: - intentional vs accidental, - negligent vs unavoidable, - provoked vs unprovoked, - foreseeable vs unforeseeable.
Prediction pattern: giving clear evidence of constraints reduces blame (shifts from “bad person” to “bad situation”).

title: Moral psychology
text:
Moralization: when preferences become sacred
Some issues become “moralized”: - disagreement feels like betrayal, - compromise feels dirty, - opponents feel dangerous.
Prediction patterns - moralized issues polarize more strongly than non-moral issues, - punishment and exclusion become more acceptable, - factual debate becomes less effective.
Intervention lever: de-moralize where possible by shifting from blame to shared goals and tradeoffs.

title: Moral psychology
text:
Norm enforcement: formal and informal
People enforce norms through: - gossip and reputation, - praise and shame, - exclusion, - punishment (private or public), - institutional enforcement (police, courts, HR, schools).
Prediction patterns - observability increases compliance and norm enforcement, - selective enforcement damages legitimacy, - unclear norms invite conflict over interpretation and power.

title: Moral psychology
text:
A reusable moral analysis template
When analyzing a moral conflict, specify:

What norm is at stake? (harm, fairness, loyalty, authority, purity?)

What intention is attributed? (hostile, negligent, accidental?)

What emotions are active? (anger, disgust, shame, guilt?)

What identity boundary is salient? (us vs them?)

What enforcement channel exists? (informal vs institutional)

Prediction: what changes if you change transparency, fairness, or face-saving options?

title: Moral psychology
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Punishment demand after perceived disrespect

small disrespect is interpreted as intentional threat,
anger rises,
punitive preference increases.

Mechanisms: threat interpretation + anger + status concern.


Example B: Legitimacy-based compliance

people comply because noncompliance feels wrong,
not just because punishment is feared.

Mechanisms: authority legitimacy + moral identity + guilt/shame.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
Sleep and stress modulate almost every mechanism in psychology: - attention and working memory, - emotion regulation, - threat sensitivity, - learning and habit expression, - social interpretation.
This page treats them as system-wide parameters rather than niche health topics.

title: Sleep & stress
section: Sleep: the cognitive and emotional regulator
text:
Sleep: the cognitive and emotional regulator
Sleep influences: - attention (vigilance, sustained focus), - working memory (multi-step reasoning), - emotion regulation (reactivity and recovery), - learning (consolidation of memories and skills).
Prediction patterns - sleep loss increases errors and impulsivity, - sleep loss increases negative affect and threat sensitivity, - complex reasoning and self-control degrade earlier than simple tasks.
Practical implication: if behavior looks “irrational” under sleep loss, it may be capacity limits rather than preference change.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
Stress: acute vs chronic

Acute stress
Acute stress often produces: - narrowed attention (“tunnel vision”), - faster but less flexible action, - reliance on habits and scripts, - increased threat interpretation.
Prediction pattern: under acute stress, people choose simpler strategies and show less deep mentalizing.


Chronic stress
Chronic stress often produces: - fatigue and reduced executive function, - irritability and negative affect, - reduced exploratory behavior, - stronger avoidance and withdrawal loops.
Prediction pattern: chronic stress shifts behavior toward short-run relief strategies.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
Threat sensitivity: the amplifier channel
A key pathway is threat detection: - when threat systems are activated, ambiguity is interpreted pessimistically, - social cues are read as hostile more often, - retaliation and defensiveness increase.
Prediction patterns - minor provocations escalate faster under stress, - distrust spreads more quickly in low-safety environments, - institutions that feel threatening reduce cooperation.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
Stress and learning: habit dominance
Stress often increases: - reliance on well-learned routines, - avoidance learning, - reinforcement of immediate relief behaviors.
Prediction pattern: in stressful environments, behavior becomes more habitual and less responsive to abstract information.

title: Sleep & stress
section: Stress and social cognition: attribution shifts
text:
Stress and social cognition: attribution shifts
Under stress, people: - mentalize less deeply, - rely more on stereotypes and categories, - commit more attribution errors (trait-blame vs situation).
Prediction pattern: conflict and polarization rise when stress is high and identity boundaries are salient.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
Interventions: what reliably helps (mechanism-first)

Reduce load

simplify tasks and choices,
reduce multitasking,
restructure environments to make the desired action easy.



Increase predictability and safety

clear procedures, stable rules,
respectful treatment (legitimacy),
face-saving options to reduce humiliation-driven escalation.



Improve recovery and regulation

consistent sleep routines,
downtime after conflict exposure,
supportive social ties and safe disclosure.

Note: these are not “motivational slogans”; they change cognitive capacity and emotional reactivity.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
A reusable analysis template
When sleep/stress may matter, ask:

State: acute vs chronic?

Capacity: attention/working memory reduced?

Emotion: threat sensitivity elevated?

Habit: are routines dominating?

Social inference: more hostile attribution likely?

Prediction: what changes if you reduce load or increase safety?

Topics: norms & groups (stress amplifies group threat dynamics)
Overlaps: institutions (procedural justice reduces threat), criminology (hot spots, escalation, legitimacy), communication (arousal-driven spread)

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
This page is a mechanism map for persistent behaviors that feel hard to stop: substance use, gambling-like reinforcement patterns, compulsive checking, and other cue-driven cycles.
It is not a diagnostic guide. The goal is to understand loops: cue → craving/urge → action → reward/relief → learning → stronger cue control.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
The core loop
A compact loop that explains many compulsive patterns:

Cue (place, emotion, people, device, time)

Urge/craving (state shift: attention narrows)

Action (routine)

Reward or relief (positive or negative reinforcement)

Learning (habit strengthens; cues gain power)

Aftermath (guilt/shame/stress may create new cues)

Many interventions work by breaking the loop at (1) or (2), not at (4).

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
Mechanism 1: Reinforcement (reward and relief)
Two reinforcement channels matter:

Positive reinforcement: behavior produces pleasure/reward.
Negative reinforcement: behavior removes discomfort (stress, anxiety, withdrawal, boredom).

Negative reinforcement is often the “stickiness engine” because relief is immediate.
Prediction patterns - stress increases craving and relapse risk (more need for relief). - delayed costs are discounted; immediate relief dominates. - inconsistent rewards can create persistent repetition.

title: Addiction & compulsion
section: Mechanism 2: Cue reactivity and attentional capture
text:
Mechanism 2: Cue reactivity and attentional capture
Over time, cues become powerful: - they trigger urges automatically, - they capture attention (“tunnel vision”), - they reduce working memory available for self-control.
Prediction patterns - exposure to cues increases cravings even without conscious intent. - “willpower” fails more in cue-rich environments.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
Mechanism 3: Habit dominance under stress
Under stress, fatigue, and sleep loss: - executive function decreases, - habits dominate, - people revert to default routines.
Prediction pattern: relapse often follows stress spikes or depletion states, even if motivation remains high.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
Mechanism 4: Identity and shame loops
After repeated failure, people can form an identity narrative: - “this is who I am,” - “I can’t change,” - “people will judge me.”
Shame often increases concealment and isolation, which reduces support and increases stress.
Prediction patterns - stigma reduces help-seeking. - social support and identity-safe environments increase sustained change.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
Mechanism 5: Social networks and norms
Behavior is shaped by: - peer availability and models, - shared routines, - norms about use and “what counts as normal.”
Prediction pattern: changing social context can matter as much as changing individual motivation.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
Interventions as loop-breaking (mechanism → lever)

Break at cues (1)

remove triggers,
change routes, routines, environments,
add friction (extra steps),
block access during vulnerable times.



Break at urge (2)

urge-surfing (delay the action),
emotion regulation strategies,
alternative relief (exercise, connection, structured activity),
“if-then” implementation intentions.



Break at action-to-reward mapping (3–4)

reduce reward intensity/availability,
increase immediate costs (commitment contracts),
replace routine with a lower-harm substitute.



Break at aftermath (6)

reduce shame and isolation,
build repair scripts (“slip ≠ collapse”),
increase support and accountability.

Key principle: if an intervention relies only on motivation, it will fail in cue-rich + high-stress environments.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
A reusable analysis template
When analyzing a compulsive pattern, specify:

Cues: what triggers it (external + internal states)?

Reinforcement: reward or relief? immediate or delayed?

Habit strength: how automatic is the routine?

Stress/sleep: what states amplify it?

Social context: who/what environment sustains it?

Loop break: which link can realistically be weakened?

title: Motivation & goals
text: Motivation determines what people try to do, how much effort they invest, and what tradeoffs they accept. Goals don’t just guide action — they also guide attention, memory, and interpretation.

title: Motivation & goals
text:
Goal types

Approach vs avoidance

Approach: pursue desirable outcomes.
Avoidance: prevent negative outcomes.

Avoidance goals can dominate attention and produce short-horizon “relief” strategies.


Mastery vs performance

Mastery: improve competence, learn.
Performance: look competent, avoid looking bad.

Prediction pattern: performance focus increases anxiety and risk-avoidance; mastery focus increases persistence and learning.

title: Motivation & goals
text:
Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation

Intrinsic: doing the task is rewarding.
Extrinsic: task is a means to an external reward.

Prediction pattern: heavy external control can reduce intrinsic engagement when it changes the meaning from “I choose” to “I’m being controlled.”

title: Motivation & goals
text:
Goal conflict and self-regulation
People often hold multiple goals that conflict: - study vs social media, - fairness vs self-interest, - honesty vs reputation.
Conflict resolution depends on: - salience (which goal is active), - state (stress/fatigue), - identity (what kind of person I am), - environment (friction/defaults).
Prediction pattern: making long-run goals salient at decision time improves alignment without changing values.

title: Motivation & goals
section: Motivation under uncertainty: expectancy × value (practical lens)
text:
Motivation under uncertainty: expectancy × value (practical lens)
Effort tends to rise with: - expectancy (belief that effort helps), - value (importance of the outcome).
Failures often come from: - low expectancy (“it won’t matter”), - unclear value (“why do this?”), - high immediate costs.
Intervention levers - increase expectancy via feedback and progress signals, - increase value via meaning/identity framing, - reduce immediate costs via environment design.

title: Motivation & goals
section: Social motivation: status, belonging, and norms
text:
Social motivation: status, belonging, and norms
People are motivated by: - approval and belonging, - status and respect, - avoidance of shame.
Prediction pattern: peer environments can outpower individual incentives.

title: Motivation & goals
text:
A reusable template
To explain motivated behavior, specify:

Which goal is active (approach/avoidance; mastery/performance)

Expectancy and value (why try?)

Immediate costs (effort, fear, shame, opportunity cost)

Identity and norms (who am I here?)

Prediction: what shifts if you change salience, feedback, or social audience?

title: Motivation & goals
text:
Connections

Self-control: motivation interacts with cues and commitment.
Emotion & motivation: emotions shift goal priority.
Norms & groups: identity and belonging shape goal choice.
Institutions: incentives work better when they align with identity and legitimacy.

title: Relationships
text:
Relationships are repeated interaction under uncertainty: - you infer intentions from ambiguous signals, - you learn from feedback that is noisy and emotionally charged, - you coordinate norms, roles, and expectations over time.
This page is mechanism-first: attachment + trust + conflict cycles → predictions.

title: Relationships
text:
A compact map
Relationships often hinge on four systems:

Attachment / security (how safe connection feels)

Trust and expectations (beliefs about reliability and goodwill)

Communication and repair (how errors are handled)

Conflict regulation (how threat and anger are managed)

title: Relationships
section: Mechanism 1: Attachment as a threat-regulation system (high-level)
text:
Mechanism 1: Attachment as a threat-regulation system (high-level)
Attachment can be treated as a system for managing: - closeness vs autonomy, - safety vs threat, - seeking support vs self-reliance.
When security is high: - ambiguity is interpreted more benignly, - repair is easier, - cooperation is more resilient.
When security is low: - threat interpretation increases, - reassurance-seeking or withdrawal increases, - conflict escalates faster.
Prediction pattern: increasing perceived safety reduces reactive cycles more reliably than “better arguments.”
(This is a descriptive mechanism lens, not a clinical taxonomy.)

title: Relationships
section: Mechanism 2: Trust is learned, but fragile
text:
Mechanism 2: Trust is learned, but fragile
Trust is a belief about: - competence (“can they do it?”), - goodwill (“do they intend good?”), - predictability (“will they act consistently?”).
Trust updates asymmetrically: - one betrayal can outweigh many cooperative acts (negativity dominance), - ambiguous signals are interpreted through prior trust levels.
Prediction patterns - low-trust relationships interpret ambiguity as hostile, - high-trust relationships interpret ambiguity as error/noise, - public accountability (clear commitments) stabilizes trust.

title: Relationships
text:
Mechanism 3: Expectations and scripts
Relationships create scripts: - who does what, - what counts as respect, - what “normal” conflict looks like, - what repair looks like.
Scripts reduce cognitive load, but: - mismatched scripts create chronic misunderstanding, - unspoken expectations create resentment.
Prediction pattern: making expectations explicit reduces conflict more than increasing “effort.”

title: Relationships
text:
Mechanism 4: Conflict cycles (the interaction loop)
Many conflicts follow a loop:

ambiguous cue → negative interpretation

emotion (anger/fear/shame) rises

defensive behavior (attack/withdraw)

partner responds defensively

loop confirms the negative model

Two common defensive styles: - pursue/attack (demand, criticize, escalate) - withdraw/avoid (silence, delay, disengage)
Neither is “the problem” alone; the loop is the problem.
Prediction patterns - under stress, loops intensify (less mentalizing, more habit), - small face-saving opportunities reduce escalation, - repair attempts work only if perceived as sincere and timely.

title: Relationships
section: Mechanism 5: Repair as a high-leverage move
text:
Mechanism 5: Repair as a high-leverage move
Repair includes: - acknowledgment of harm, - credible explanation (not excuse), - commitment to change, - restitution/compensation, - emotional validation.
Repair works by shifting: - beliefs (“they care / they understand”), - emotions (reduced threat), - norms (“we fix things like this”).
Prediction pattern: repair is most effective when it happens early (before narratives harden).

title: Relationships
text:
Mechanism 6: Power, dependence, and asymmetry
Dependence shapes behavior: - the more dependent partner may accommodate more, - the less dependent partner may set norms.
Power differences can distort communication: - fear of consequences reduces honesty, - disagreement becomes costly, - concealment and resentment grow.
Prediction pattern: reducing fear and increasing safe voice increases truth-telling and cooperation.

title: Relationships
text:
A reusable relationship analysis template
To analyze a relationship dynamic, specify:

Uncertainty: what is ambiguous and how is it interpreted?

Security: does the system feel safe or threatening?

Trust: competence, goodwill, predictability—where is it weak?

Scripts: what expectations are implicit vs explicit?

Cycle: what is the repeating loop (attack/withdraw, criticism/defense)?

Repair: what intervention would interrupt the loop?

title: Relationships
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Misinterpretation → escalation

one side interprets delay as disrespect,
responds with criticism,
other withdraws,
criticism increases.

Mechanisms: attribution + threat sensitivity + pursue/withdraw loop.


Example B: Trust stabilization via commitments

clear commitments reduce ambiguity,
follow-through produces predictable feedback,
trust increases over time.

Mechanisms: credibility + learning + norm stabilization.

text:
Connections

Foundations: social cognition (intent inference), emotion & motivation (anger/shame/guilt), communication (credibility/repair), learning (trust updates), sleep & stress (amplifier)
Topics: norms & groups (relationship norms), personality (heterogeneity), biases (interpretation errors)
