title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Beliefs are internal models of the world: what is true, how likely it is, and what causes what.
This page focuses on how beliefs form and change under limited information, limited attention, and social influence.
A key theme: > People update beliefs using evidence and psychological constraints (salience, identity, emotion, trust).

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Three objects to track
When discussing beliefs, separate:

Level: what do I think is true?

Uncertainty: how sure am I?

Calibration: does confidence match accuracy?

Many disputes are really disputes about (2) and (3).

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Sources of belief
Beliefs come from: - personal experience, - testimony and communication, - institutions (official reports, rules, signals), - social networks and norms, - memory (which is reconstructive).
Prediction pattern: beliefs become “sticky” when they are tied to identity or repeated through social reinforcement.

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
section: Updating under uncertainty: why it deviates from ideal Bayesian updating
text:
Updating under uncertainty: why it deviates from ideal Bayesian updating
Even when people try to be rational, updating is constrained by:

1) Salience and availability
Evidence that is vivid, recent, or emotionally charged is overweighted.
Prediction pattern: salient events produce spikes in perceived risk that decay over time.


2) Selective attention and selective exposure
People seek information that fits goals and identity, and avoid costly dissonance.
Prediction pattern: information diets become polarized even without explicit propaganda.


3) Asymmetric skepticism
People scrutinize disconfirming evidence more harshly than confirming evidence.
Prediction pattern: mixed evidence can increase confidence rather than reduce it (biased assimilation).


4) Trust and source credibility
People treat sources as part of the data: - “Is this person competent?” - “Are they honest?” - “Are they on my side?”
Prediction pattern: same facts produce different belief change across trust groups.

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Causal beliefs: stories beat statistics
People strongly prefer causal narratives: - “X caused Y because …” - “This type of person does …” - “This policy leads to …”
Causal learning is hard when: - multiple causes move together, - feedback is delayed, - systems adapt strategically.
Prediction pattern: people overinfer causality from small samples and salient coincidences.

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Confidence: the underappreciated variable
Confidence drives behavior: - willingness to act, - willingness to punish, - willingness to speak, - openness to learning.
But confidence is often miscalibrated.

Overconfidence and underconfidence

Overconfidence can produce excessive risk-taking or premature commitment.
Underconfidence can produce paralysis and overreliance on authority.

Prediction pattern: reducing uncertainty (clearer feedback, better measurement) changes behavior even if belief levels don’t move much.

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Metacognition: knowing what you know
Metacognition is the ability to monitor: - how accurate you are, - when you’re guessing, - when you need more information.
Metacognition degrades under: - stress, - time pressure, - strong emotion, - social threat.
Prediction pattern: hostile environments reduce honest uncertainty expression (“everyone must sound certain”).

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
section: Social belief dynamics: cascades and pluralistic ignorance
text:
Social belief dynamics: cascades and pluralistic ignorance
Beliefs spread socially, sometimes creating: - information cascades: people copy others because they assume others know more. - pluralistic ignorance: people privately disagree but assume others agree, so they stay silent.
Prediction patterns - Public signals can trigger rapid belief shifts. - Small visible minorities can shape perceived norms disproportionately.

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
A reusable belief analysis template
When explaining belief formation or change, specify:

Evidence: what information exists and who sees it?

Trust: which sources are credible to whom?

Salience: what is vivid vs statistical?

Identity: what beliefs are socially rewarded?

Uncertainty: how confident are people, and is it calibrated?

Feedback: is correction fast, slow, or absent?

Prediction: what changes if you change visibility, messenger, or feedback?

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Connections

Learning: beliefs update differently from habits; both matter.
Decision-making: confidence and uncertainty shape risk and action.
Communication overlap: trust, framing, and identity determine belief change.
Criminology overlap: perceived risk, legitimacy, and rumor dynamics drive cooperation and compliance.

title: Measurement
text:
Measurement is where many psychological arguments succeed or fail.
If you want to claim “X affects Y,” you must know: - what X and Y mean operationally, - whether they are measured reliably, - whether your measure captures the construct rather than noise.
This page is deeper than Methods: it’s about how variables are built.

title: Measurement
text:
Constructs vs measures
A construct is the idea (e.g., “trust”, “self-control”, “anxiety”).
A measure is the operational tool (survey items, tasks, behavior logs).
One construct can have many measures, and one measure can mix constructs.
Rule: never argue from labels. Argue from operational definitions.

title: Measurement
section: Validity: are you measuring what you think?
text:
Validity: are you measuring what you think?

Content validity
Does the measure cover the construct’s important aspects?


Convergent / discriminant validity

Convergent: does it correlate with other measures of the same construct?
Discriminant: does it avoid correlating with unrelated constructs?



Predictive validity
Does it predict outcomes the construct should predict?
Red flag: a measure is used because it is popular, not because it is justified for the specific argument.

title: Measurement
section: Reliability: is the measure stable enough to be useful?
text:
Reliability: is the measure stable enough to be useful?

Internal consistency (for multi-item scales)
Are items measuring the same underlying thing?


Test–retest reliability
Does the measure remain similar over time (when it should)?


Inter-rater reliability
When humans rate behavior, do they agree?
Practical implication: low reliability makes effects look unstable and encourages overfitting.

title: Measurement
text:
Self-report: useful but not “direct access”
Self-report captures: - introspection, - self-image, - social desirability, - memory reconstruction.
It can be excellent for private experiences, but it also has predictable distortions.
Prediction patterns - sensitive topics are underreported in low-trust settings. - social desirability rises when anonymity is low. - current mood biases reports (“state contamination”).
Design levers - anonymity and privacy, - neutral wording, - indirect questioning when appropriate, - multiple methods (triangulation).

title: Measurement
section: Behavioral tasks: what you gain and what you risk
text:
Behavioral tasks: what you gain and what you risk
Tasks can reduce self-presentation bias but may be sensitive to: - instructions and framing, - motivation and effort, - learning during the task, - “task impurity” (multiple mechanisms affect performance).
Rule of thumb: interpret tasks as measures of performance under specific conditions, not pure traits.

title: Measurement
section: Physiological measures: strong signals, hard interpretation
text:
Physiological measures: strong signals, hard interpretation
Physiology (heart rate, skin conductance, etc.) can indicate arousal but rarely maps 1:1 to a single emotion.
Pitfall: “arousal = fear” (often false).

title: Measurement
text:
Measurement invariance (cross-group comparability)
If you compare groups (cultures, genders, age), ask: - do items mean the same thing? - do response styles differ (acquiescence, extremity, modesty)?
Prediction pattern: apparent group differences can be measurement artifacts.

title: Measurement
text:
Common measurement errors (and fixes)

Range restriction
If everyone scores near the top or bottom, correlations shrink.


Floor/ceiling effects
The measure can’t detect change.


Reactivity
Measuring behavior changes behavior (people perform for the measure).


Demand characteristics
People infer the hypothesis and comply or resist.
Fix set: pretest, blind conditions, unobtrusive outcomes, manipulate checks, and triangulate.

title: Measurement
text:
A practical checklist
Before using a variable, write:

Construct definition (one sentence)

Operationalization (exact items/task/behavior)

Reliability evidence (or why it’s acceptable without it)

Validity argument (why this measure matches the construct)

Likely biases (social desirability, reactivity, invariance)

A robustness plan (alternate measures or sensitivity tests)

title: Measurement
text:
Connections

Methods: measurement quality determines inference quality.
Mental health / stigma: self-report is especially fragile under shame/fear.
Criminology: reporting and enforcement are measurement systems with selection bias.
Institutions: procedural justice shapes willingness to report truthfully.

title: Person perception
text:
Person perception is how we form impressions: who is trustworthy, dangerous, competent, or worth listening to. It drives hiring, friendship, conflict, stigma, authority legitimacy, and persuasion.
This page is about rapid inference under uncertainty.

title: Person perception
text:
Two core dimensions (practical, not absolute)
A lot of impressions can be summarized as: - Warmth: intent toward me/us (friend or threat?) - Competence: ability to act (capable or ineffective?)
These shape: - trust and cooperation (warmth), - deference and reliance (competence).
Prediction pattern: changing perceived intent often moves behavior more than changing perceived ability.

title: Person perception
text:
Thin slices and cue use
People infer from: - facial expression, tone, posture, - clothing, group markers, - fluency and confidence, - context (roles: “police”, “doctor”, “student”).
Thin-slice inference can be useful but error-prone.
Prediction pattern: under time pressure, people rely more on surface cues and stereotypes.

title: Person perception
text:
Attribution: intent vs constraint
Judgment often depends on: - perceived intentionality, - perceived constraints, - perceived controllability.
Prediction pattern: providing situational constraints reduces blame and moralized judgment.

title: Person perception
text:
Stereotypes as low-cost representations
Stereotypes reduce cognitive load but can become self-reinforcing: - selective attention to confirming evidence, - misinterpretation of ambiguous behavior, - avoidance reduces counter-evidence.
Prediction pattern: increasing cross-group contact under safe conditions reduces reliance on stereotypes.

title: Person perception
text:
Trust cues and credibility heuristics
People judge credibility using: - track record, expertise, institutional role, - confidence and fluency, - in-group membership.
Pitfall: fluency and confidence can be mistaken for truth.
Prediction pattern: trusted messengers outperform stronger arguments from distrusted messengers.

title: Person perception
text:
Error patterns to watch

Halo effect: one positive trait colors others.
Negativity dominance: one bad signal outweighs many good ones.
Fundamental attribution tendency: trait-blame over situation.
Out-group homogeneity: “they are all the same.”

title: Person perception
text:
A reusable template
When analyzing person perception, specify:

What cues are visible and salient

Warmth/intent inference vs competence/ability inference

Situational constraints that are ignored or unseen

Group boundaries (identity)

Prediction: what shifts with more time, more context, or different messenger?

title: Person perception
text:
Connections

Social cognition: theory of mind + attribution.
Communication: credibility, persuasion, distrust.
Norms & groups: identity shapes interpretation.
Criminology: legitimacy, threat interpretation, escalation.

title: Topics
text:
Topics are reusable “modules” you can plug into many explanations.
They sit on top of Foundations (cognition, learning, decision-making, emotion, social cognition, methods).

title: Topics
text:
How to use Topics
For any topic page, try the same template: 1) Mechanism(s)
2) Predictions (what changes when the environment changes?)
3) Failure modes (when the explanation breaks)
4) Interventions (what reliably shifts behavior?)
5) Links to Foundations and Overlaps

title: Mental health
text:
This page is a foundational, non-clinical map of mental health topics that matter for understanding behavior. It is not a diagnostic guide. The goal is to organize mechanisms and predictions in a way that is useful for study and for linking to other parts of the site (decision-making, learning, emotion, social cognition).
A helpful framing: > Mental health patterns often reflect interactions between vulnerabilities, environments, and coping strategies.

title: Mental health
text:
Core dimensions (a practical map)
Many symptoms can be grouped by a few dimensions:

Negative affect: persistent sadness, anxiety, guilt, irritability
Threat sensitivity: hypervigilance, avoidance, panic responses
Reward processing: reduced pleasure, low motivation, anhedonia
Cognitive control: attention, impulsivity, rumination, executive function
Sleep and arousal: insomnia, fatigue, agitation
Social functioning: isolation, mistrust, rejection sensitivity

Different “disorders” often share dimensions. That’s part of why comorbidity is common.

title: Mental health
section: Stress and vulnerability: a general mechanism
text:
Stress and vulnerability: a general mechanism
A broad mechanism often used is:

Vulnerability (traits, history, genetics, learned patterns)
Stressors (acute shocks, chronic strain, social conflict)
Protective factors (support, coping skills, stable routines)

Prediction pattern: the same stressor affects people differently depending on vulnerability and protection.

title: Mental health
text:
Anxiety: threat and uncertainty
Anxiety is often characterized by: - heightened threat perception, - intolerance of uncertainty, - avoidance behavior, - safety-seeking behaviors that reduce anxiety short-run but maintain it long-run.
Learning loop (common): - uncertainty → anxiety → avoidance → temporary relief → stronger avoidance habit
Prediction pattern: reducing avoidance and increasing safe exposure often weakens the loop over time (mechanism: learning + prediction error).

title: Mental health
text:
Depression: reward, energy, and self-evaluation
Depressive patterns often involve: - reduced motivation and energy, - diminished reward sensitivity (things feel less rewarding), - negative self-evaluation, - rumination (repetitive negative thinking).
Behavioral loop (common): - low mood → withdrawal → fewer rewarding experiences → lower mood
Prediction pattern: small increases in structured rewarding activity can have outsized effects because they interrupt the loop (mechanism: reinforcement and habit).

title: Mental health
section: Rumination: repetitive thought as a trap
text:
Rumination: repetitive thought as a trap
Rumination feels like problem-solving but often functions as: - attention capture, - negative memory retrieval, - threat rehearsal, - reduced action initiation.
Prediction pattern: interventions that shift attention (structured activity, reappraisal skills, sleep stabilization) reduce rumination frequency.

title: Mental health
section: Trauma-related patterns: memory, threat, and triggers
text:
Trauma-related patterns: memory, threat, and triggers
After extreme stress, some people develop: - intrusive memories, - hypervigilance, - avoidance of reminders, - emotional numbing, - sleep disruption.
Mechanism lens: emotion-tagged memory + threat system sensitization + avoidance learning.
Prediction pattern: unpredictable triggers and uncertain environments maintain hypervigilance.

title: Mental health
text:
ADHD-like patterns (non-diagnostic framing)
Common behavioral dimensions include: - inattention under low stimulation, - difficulty sustaining effort, - impulsivity (short-horizon choice), - strong sensitivity to immediate rewards.
Mechanism lens: attention regulation + reinforcement sensitivity + executive control load.
Prediction pattern: structure, feedback frequency, and reduced friction can help performance even without changing “traits.”

title: Mental health
section: Substance use and compulsive behavior (mechanism lens)
text:
Substance use and compulsive behavior (mechanism lens)
A compact mechanism view: - strong immediate reward/relief, - habit formation, - cue-triggered craving, - withdrawal/negative reinforcement, - social context and norms.
Prediction pattern: changing cue environments and social networks often matters as much as willpower.

title: Mental health
text:
Stigma and social context (often overlooked)
Mental health is shaped by: - perceived acceptance vs rejection, - shame and concealment, - access to support and care, - institutional treatment (school, workplace, legal system).
Prediction pattern: reducing stigma and increasing safe disclosure channels increases help-seeking and reduces isolation loops.

title: Mental health
text:
A reusable explanation template
When discussing a mental health-related behavior, specify:

Dimension(s) involved (threat, reward, control, sleep, social)
Loop (avoidance loop? withdrawal loop? rumination loop?)
Context (stressors, stability, social support)
Prediction (what change would interrupt the loop?)
Boundaries (what you are not claiming; avoid diagnosis)

title: Mental health
text:
Connections

Emotion & motivation: affective systems and action tendencies are central.
Learning: avoidance and reinforcement loops maintain patterns.
Cognition: attention and memory biases shape symptoms.
Norms & groups: stigma and identity can worsen or buffer outcomes.
Criminology (later link): trauma exposure, substance use, and stress can affect compliance, escalation, and institutional interactions.

title: Personality
text:
Personality is about stable individual differences in how people think, feel, and behave across time and situations.
A clean stance for notes: - People differ (traits are real and predictive), - Situations matter (context can amplify or suppress traits), - The interesting part is person × situation.

title: Personality
text:
What personality is (in practice)
Personality is typically measured using: - questionnaires (self-report), - informant reports, - behavioral tasks, - digital traces (with caution).
Traits are not “destiny,” but they are: - moderately stable, - meaningfully predictive, - useful for explaining heterogeneity.

title: Personality
text:
The Big Five (high-level map)
A common organizing framework uses five broad dimensions:

Openness: curiosity, imagination, preference for novelty/complexity
Conscientiousness: self-control, planning, persistence, reliability
Extraversion: social energy, assertiveness, positive affect
Agreeableness: cooperation, empathy, conflict avoidance
Neuroticism (emotional instability): sensitivity to threat, negative affect

These are not the only model, but they’re a practical baseline.
Prediction pattern: these traits correlate with typical life outcomes (health behaviors, relationship stability, work patterns), but effects depend strongly on environment.

title: Personality
section: Traits vs states vs skills (avoid a common confusion)
text:
Traits vs states vs skills (avoid a common confusion)

Trait: stable tendency (baseline).
State: temporary condition (stress, fatigue, mood).
Skill: learned capability (self-regulation strategies, social skills).

A person can have: - low baseline self-control (trait), - but strong self-regulation skills (skill), - and still fail under extreme stress (state).

title: Personality
text:
Person × situation: why “traits sometimes disappear”
Behavior is shaped by: - trait tendencies, - incentives and constraints, - norms and roles, - salience and emotional state.
Two environments can produce different behavior from the same person: - in one setting, the trait is expressed, - in another, it’s suppressed by norms or constraints.
Prediction pattern: strong situations (strict rules, high surveillance, high stakes) reduce observed personality differences.

title: Personality
text:
Mechanisms: how personality “shows up”
Traits influence behavior through: - attention (what cues you notice), - interpretation (what stories you tell about events), - emotion (how strongly you react), - habits (default routines), - social strategy (approach/avoid conflict, seek status, seek belonging).
This keeps personality from being “just labels.”

title: Personality
text:
Conscientiousness as the workhorse trait (often)
Conscientiousness is especially linked to: - long-run planning, - persistence, - reliability, - lower impulsivity.
Prediction pattern: in many domains, conscientiousness moderates the impact of present bias and temptation.
Interventions note: skills + environment often outperform “changing the trait.” Examples: - reminders, checklists, friction reduction, - commitment devices, - predictable routines.

title: Personality
section: Dark-side traits and antisocial patterns (careful framing)
text:
Dark-side traits and antisocial patterns (careful framing)
Some personality patterns are associated with: - low empathy, - impulsivity, - antagonism, - thrill-seeking, - manipulativeness.
Use caution: - avoid moralizing labels as explanations, - specify mechanisms (emotion regulation, threat perception, reinforcement history), - distinguish trait disposition from situational triggers.

title: Personality
text:
Measurement cautions (methods-minded)

Self-report is sensitive to self-image and social desirability.
Traits can be distorted by current mood/state.
Cross-cultural measurement invariance matters (same questions may not mean the same thing).

Rule of thumb: treat trait measures as informative but noisy; triangulate when possible.

title: Personality
text:
A reusable explanation template
When using personality in an explanation:

Which trait dimension is relevant?

Which mechanism connects the trait to behavior (attention, emotion, habit, strategy)?

What situation features amplify/suppress expression (rules, monitoring, threat, incentives)?

What prediction follows (who changes behavior under which intervention)?

title: Personality
text:
Connections

Decision-making: personality affects risk tolerance, patience, and self-control expression.
Emotion & motivation: neuroticism relates to threat sensitivity; extraversion relates to positive affect and approach.
Social cognition: agreeableness affects trust and conflict interpretation.
Criminology: trait heterogeneity matters (impulsivity, self-control, antagonism), but should be modeled alongside environment and institutions.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Biases are systematic patterns in judgment and choice. A useful framing:
This page is organized as mechanism → prediction rather than a long list.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Two categories that prevent confusion

Judgment vs choice

Judgment biases: errors in beliefs (probabilities, frequencies, causal stories).
Choice biases: shifts in preferences or decisions due to framing, defaults, and context.

A pattern can be both.


Bias vs noise

Bias: systematic direction (predictable).
Noise: randomness (unpredictable variability).

Reducing noise is often easier than “removing” bias.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 1: Availability (retrieval-driven judgment)
People judge frequency/risk by what comes to mind easily.
Prediction patterns - vivid events feel more common than they are, - recent events dominate risk perception, - repeated exposure increases perceived truth (“familiarity = credibility”).
Common pitfall: interpreting availability as “irrational” when the environment is genuinely changing (recency may be informative).

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 2: Representativeness (pattern-matching)
People assess likelihood by similarity to a stereotype or prototype.
Prediction patterns - base rates are neglected when similarity cues are strong, - small samples are treated as representative (overconfidence), - people see “streaks” in randomness.
Testable intervention: making base rates salient reduces the effect.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 3: Anchoring (starting-point dependence)
Numerical judgments are pulled toward an initial value, even if arbitrary.
Prediction patterns - first numbers in negotiation or estimation shape outcomes, - adjustments are insufficient, especially under time pressure.
Intervention: generate your own anchor first, or force multiple independent estimates.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 4: Framing (representation changes choice)
Equivalent descriptions can change the perceived problem.
Prediction patterns - gains vs losses change risk-taking, - “per 100 people” vs “percentage” changes intuitions, - order and grouping of options change perceived attractiveness.
Practical note: framing is often more about attention and categorization than deep preference change.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 5: Confirmation and asymmetric skepticism
People search for evidence that supports what they already think, and scrutinize opposing evidence more harshly.
Prediction patterns - polarization increases with identity-relevant topics, - mixed evidence leads to stronger prior beliefs (biased assimilation), - people become more confident after consuming selective information.
Intervention: force consideration of strong counterarguments; pre-commit to what evidence would change your mind.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 6: Overconfidence and miscalibration
People often overestimate accuracy and underestimate uncertainty.
Prediction patterns - too-narrow confidence intervals, - “illusion of control” in noisy environments, - planning fallacy (systematic underestimation of time/cost).
Intervention: reference class forecasting (use similar past projects as priors).

title: Biases & heuristics
section: Mechanism 7: Status quo, defaults, and friction
text:
Mechanism 7: Status quo, defaults, and friction
Doing nothing is often a decision rule.
Prediction patterns - defaults dominate choices when attention is scarce, - small “hassle costs” change behavior a lot, - opt-in vs opt-out designs shift participation dramatically.
Interpretation: not necessarily preference; often an attention/effort allocation outcome.

title: Biases & heuristics
section: Mechanism 8: Affect and arousal (emotion as a driver)
text:
Mechanism 8: Affect and arousal (emotion as a driver)
Feelings shape what seems risky, urgent, or morally acceptable.
Prediction patterns - fear increases threat sensitivity and avoidance, - anger increases punitive choices and perceived intentionality, - stress increases habit reliance and narrows attention.
Links: this connects directly to Emotion & motivation.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
A compact “bias debugging” checklist
When you see a bias-like pattern, ask: 1) Attention: what information is salient vs hidden? 2) Memory: what examples come to mind? 3) Computation: is the task too complex for working memory? 4) Feedback: is learning noisy, delayed, or selective? 5) Identity/emotion: is the topic threatening or status-relevant? 6) Choice architecture: are defaults/friction doing the work?
If changing (1), (3), or (5) changes behavior, it’s likely not a stable preference.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Connections to other pages

Cognition: biases often come from attention, memory, and representation limits.
Decision-making: biases shape both judgment and choice.
Social cognition: identity and norms amplify confirmation and attribution patterns.
Criminology: measurement, reporting, and enforcement contexts interact with bias and salience.

title: Development
text:
Development is about how psychological mechanisms change across the life course: - cognitive capacity and control, - learning styles and sensitivity to reward/punishment, - social reasoning and identity, - emotion regulation and stress reactivity.
This page is a mechanism map you can reuse when thinking about age, cohorts, schooling, family, and peer environments.

title: Development
text:
A practical stance
Instead of treating “age” as a label, treat it as a bundle of changing parameters:

capacity (attention, working memory, executive control)
experience (learned scripts, habits, domain knowledge)
motivation (goals, identity, status)
context (family, school/work, peers, institutions)
plasticity (how quickly learning happens; sensitivity to feedback)

title: Development
section: Mechanism 1: Executive function and self-control develop (then decline later)
text:
Mechanism 1: Executive function and self-control develop (then decline later)
Self-control is strongly linked to: - attention regulation, - inhibition, - planning, - working memory.
In many people: - executive control increases through childhood/adolescence into early adulthood, - then can decline later with aging, depending on health and context.
Prediction patterns - impulsive choices are more common when executive control is still developing, especially under stress. - structure and routines help when control capacity is limited. - environments with strong cues and temptations amplify control differences.

title: Development
section: Mechanism 2: Reward sensitivity and novelty seeking
text:
Mechanism 2: Reward sensitivity and novelty seeking
Many adolescent/young-adult environments involve: - heightened sensitivity to social reward, - stronger status incentives, - stronger novelty seeking.
This is not only “immaturity”; it can be adaptive for exploration, but risky under certain environments.
Prediction patterns - peer presence increases risk-taking more for younger individuals than older adults. - interventions that change social reward (status, approval) can be more effective than purely informational warnings.

title: Development
section: Mechanism 3: Social cognition and identity formation
text:
Mechanism 3: Social cognition and identity formation
Social cognition becomes more sophisticated over time, but identity pressures also rise: - belonging and status needs can dominate, - group norms become highly salient.
Prediction patterns - identity threats amplify motivated reasoning and conformity. - in-group messengers and identity-safe framing matter more in identity-sensitive periods.

title: Development
section: Mechanism 4: Learning and habit formation across stages
text:
Mechanism 4: Learning and habit formation across stages
People learn through reinforcement, imitation, instruction, and practice. But: - early experiences can set durable scripts (“what relationships are like,” “what authority is like”), - repeated environments create habits that persist even after beliefs change.
Prediction patterns - early consistent feedback shapes stable expectations (trust vs threat). - inconsistent or unpredictable environments increase vigilance and short-horizon choice. - habit change is harder when environments remain cue-rich.

title: Development
section: Mechanism 5: Family, peers, and institutions as developmental environments
text:
Mechanism 5: Family, peers, and institutions as developmental environments
Development is not only “inside the person”; it is shaped by: - parenting styles and family stability, - peer networks and norms, - school/work structures, - exposure to stress and safety, - institutional legitimacy and fairness.
Prediction patterns - stable, predictable environments support long-horizon planning and emotion regulation. - chronic threat environments increase vigilance, distrust, and reactive responses.

title: Development
text:
Mechanism 6: Sensitive periods and plasticity (high-level)
Some skills and patterns are easier to shape during windows when: - learning rates are high, - scripts are not yet rigid, - identity is still forming.
Prediction patterns - early interventions can have high returns when they change routines and peer norms. - later change is still possible, but often requires environment redesign and sustained practice.

title: Development
text:
A reusable development analysis template
When age or life stage matters, specify:

Which capacity is changing? (control, attention, social cognition, reward sensitivity)

Which environment dominates? (family, peers, school/work, institutions)

What feedback loops exist? (reward, punishment, reputation, stigma)

What is the predicted direction? (more exploration? more conformity? more threat sensitivity?)

Which intervention lever fits the stage? (structure, peer norms, identity, commitment, support)

title: Development
text:
Connections

Foundations: cognition, learning, self-control, emotion & motivation, social cognition
Topics: norms & groups, relationships, sleep & stress
Overlaps: institutions (schools, justice systems), criminology (peer effects, life-course patterns, hot states)

title: Norms & groups
text:
Groups change psychology. People do not only act as individuals; they act as members of “us” and “them,” under shared expectations about what is normal and what is acceptable.
This page is organized as: identity + norms + social dynamics → predictions.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Core concepts

Groups and identity
A group can be defined by: - membership (formal or informal), - shared symbols (language, style, rituals), - shared fate (common outcomes), - shared narratives (“who we are”).
Identity is the psychological meaning of group membership: - it shapes attention (what matters), - it shapes belief credibility (who is trusted), - it shapes motivation (what feels worth doing), - it shapes emotion (pride, shame, anger).


Norms
Norms are shared expectations about behavior.
Two useful types: - Descriptive norms: what people actually do (“most people recycle”). - Injunctive norms: what people approve (“people should recycle”).
They can move in different directions.
Pitfall: using one as evidence for the other.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Mechanism 1: Conformity and informational reliance
People conform for at least two reasons: - Informational: “Others probably know something I don’t.” - Social: “I want approval / I want to avoid rejection.”
Prediction patterns - Conformity increases with uncertainty and ambiguity. - Conformity increases when the group is cohesive and salient. - Conformity decreases when private dissent feels safe.
Intervention levers - make independent judgment easier (private responses), - increase clarity (reduce ambiguity), - highlight diversity of behavior (break false consensus).

title: Norms & groups
section: Mechanism 2: Social identity and in-group favoritism
text:
Mechanism 2: Social identity and in-group favoritism
Once “us vs them” is salient, people often: - interpret in-group behavior more charitably, - interpret out-group behavior more suspiciously, - allocate benefits to in-group members, - enforce harsher standards on out-groups.
Prediction patterns - Shared identity salience increases cooperation inside the group. - Strong subgroup identity can increase intergroup hostility. - Threat cues amplify “us vs them” categorization.
Intervention levers - superordinate identity (“we are all part of …”), - cross-cutting ties (friendships across groups), - institutional norms that reward fairness across boundaries.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Mechanism 3: Polarization and motivated reasoning (group-based)
Group identity can shape beliefs: - People accept in-group narratives more readily. - Evidence from out-group sources is discounted. - Mixed evidence can increase confidence rather than reduce it (biased assimilation).
Prediction patterns - Polarization rises when status or moral identity is threatened. - Argument quality matters less than source identity in highly polarized contexts. - “Correcting misinformation” can backfire if it signals out-group dominance.
Intervention levers - trusted in-group messengers, - identity-safe framing (“you can believe X and still be one of us”), - shared goals that reorient attention to outcomes.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Mechanism 4: Norm enforcement and punishment
Groups often sustain norms through: - gossip, - praise/shame, - exclusion, - punishment.
This can support prosocial behavior, but it can also produce rigidity and scapegoating.
Prediction patterns - Enforcement increases when behavior is observable. - Enforcement is stronger when violations signal disrespect or threat. - If institutions are seen as illegitimate, informal enforcement rises (sometimes violently).
Intervention levers - increase procedural fairness (legitimacy), - make pro-social behavior visible, - reduce ambiguous “gray-zone” rules that invite selective punishment.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Mechanism 5: Social dilemmas (cooperation problems)
Many group outcomes involve: - individual incentives to free-ride, - collective need for cooperation, - difficulty monitoring contributions.
Prediction patterns - Cooperation increases with repeated interaction and observability. - Cooperation increases when norms are salient and shared identity is strong. - Cooperation collapses when people believe others are defecting (expectation cascades).
Intervention levers - transparency (credible monitoring), - low-cost signals of commitment, - “conditional cooperation” design (make cooperation the default once enough others do).

title: Norms & groups
text:
A reusable explanation template
To explain a group outcome, specify:

Group boundaries: who is “us” vs “them”?

Norms: what is descriptive vs injunctive?

Observability: who sees what?

Sanctions: how are norms enforced (formal vs informal)?

Threat & status: is identity/status at stake?

Prediction: what shifts if identity/norm salience changes?

title: Norms & groups
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: False consensus / pluralistic ignorance

Many privately disagree with a norm.
Everyone believes others support it.
Public conformity persists.

Mechanisms: social fear + misperceived descriptive norms.


Example B: Escalation between groups

ambiguous act → hostile interpretation,
retaliation → confirms hostility,
norms shift toward aggression.

Mechanisms: threat sensitivity + attribution + norm enforcement.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Connections

Social cognition: identity shapes inference and trust.
Emotion & motivation: shame, pride, anger drive norm enforcement.
Criminology: legitimacy, trust, reporting, retaliation, and community enforcement all hinge on norms and group identity.
Overlap pages: strategic interaction becomes psychologically richer once identity and norms enter the utility function.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
A fixed point of a function \(f:X\to X\) is a point \(x^*\) such that \[
f(x^*)=x^*.
\]
Intuition. An equilibrium is often a fixed point: if “best response” maps strategies into strategies, equilibrium is where nothing changes.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
A fixed point of a function \(f:X\to X\) is a point \(x^*\) such that \[
f(x^*)=x^*.
\]
Intuition. An equilibrium is often a fixed point: if “best response” maps strategies into strategies, equilibrium is where nothing changes.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Brouwer (idea)
Brouwer’s fixed point theorem (informal): a continuous function from a compact convex set to itself has a fixed point.
This supports existence of equilibrium in many continuous games.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Correspondences (set-valued maps)
A correspondence \(F:X \rightrightarrows X\) assigns a set \(F(x)\) to each \(x\). Best responses are usually correspondences: \[
BR_i(s_{-i}) = \arg\max_{s_i\in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}),
\] which may contain multiple maximizers.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Kakutani (idea)
Kakutani’s theorem (informal): under continuity-like conditions and nonempty convex values, a correspondence has a fixed point: \[
x^* \in F(x^*).
\]
This is the classic route to Nash existence with mixed strategies: the product of best-response correspondences has a fixed point.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Example: fixed point intuition in 1D
Let \(f(x)=\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{4}\) on \([0,1]\). Solve \(x=f(x)\): \[
x=\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{4}\Rightarrow x^*=\frac{1}{2}.
\]
Equilibrium-as-fixed-point is exactly this: apply the rule, you land back on yourself.

title: Probability
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over actions. If the action set is finite, this is just a probability vector (see the simplex definition in Linear algebra).
Intuition. “Randomizing” in game theory is not mystical: it’s a distribution that other players can form beliefs about.

title: Probability
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over actions. If the action set is finite, this is just a probability vector (see the simplex definition in Linear algebra).
Intuition. “Randomizing” in game theory is not mystical: it’s a distribution that other players can form beliefs about.

title: Probability
text:
Expectation
If a random variable \(X\) takes values \(x_k\) with probabilities \(p_k\), then
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_k x_k p_k.
\]
In games, expected utility under a mixed strategy is exactly this idea: average the payoff over all possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities.

title: Probability
text:
Bayes’ rule
For events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\),
\[
\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\,\mathbb{P}(A)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}.
\]
Intuition. Prior belief \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) gets updated by how well \(A\) predicts the evidence \(B\).

title: Probability
text:
Example: updating beliefs about types
A player is either type \(H\) or \(L\). Prior \(\mathbb{P}(H)=0.3\), \(\mathbb{P}(L)=0.7\). You observe a signal \(s\). Suppose
\[
\mathbb{P}(s\mid H)=0.8,\qquad \mathbb{P}(s\mid L)=0.2.
\]
First compute the overall likelihood of \(s\):
\[
\mathbb{P}(s)=\mathbb{P}(s\mid H)\mathbb{P}(H)+\mathbb{P}(s\mid L)\mathbb{P}(L)=0.8\cdot 0.3+0.2\cdot 0.7=0.38.
\]
Then the posterior belief is
\[
\mathbb{P}(H\mid s)=\frac{0.8\cdot 0.3}{0.38}\approx 0.6316.
\]
So after observing \(s\), belief in type \(H\) rises from \(0.3\) to about \(0.63\).

title: Optimization
text:
A best response is an optimization problem. Given others’ strategies \(s_{-i}\), player \(i\) chooses
\[
BR_i(s_{-i})\in \arg\max_{s_i\in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}).
\]
Intuition. A Nash equilibrium is a fixed point of best responses: everyone is already choosing an argmax given others.

title: Optimization
text:
A best response is an optimization problem. Given others’ strategies \(s_{-i}\), player \(i\) chooses
\[
BR_i(s_{-i})\in \arg\max_{s_i\in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}).
\]
Intuition. A Nash equilibrium is a fixed point of best responses: everyone is already choosing an argmax given others.

title: Optimization
text:
FOC / SOC (unconstrained)
If \(f\) is differentiable and you maximize over an interval, an interior optimum \(x^*\) satisfies the first-order condition (FOC)
\[
f'(x^*)=0.
\]
If \(f\) is twice differentiable, the second-order condition (SOC) for a local maximum is
\[
f''(x^*)<0.
\]
Intuition. FOC finds stationary points; SOC checks that the curve bends downward.

title: Optimization
text:
KKT conditions (constrained)
For maximizing \(f(x)\) subject to inequality constraints \(g_j(x)\le 0\), define the Lagrangian
\[
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\sum_{j}\lambda_j g_j(x),
\qquad \lambda_j\ge 0.
\]
KKT conditions (at an optimum, under standard regularity assumptions) include: - Stationarity: \(\nabla_x \mathcal{L}(x^*,\lambda^*)=0\) - Primal feasibility: \(g_j(x^*)\le 0\) - Dual feasibility: \(\lambda_j^*\ge 0\) - Complementary slackness: \(\lambda_j^* g_j(x^*)=0\) for all \(j\)
Intuition. Constraints either bind (then they get a positive “shadow price” \(\lambda_j\)) or don’t bind (then \(\lambda_j=0\)).

title: Optimization
section: Example: best response with a constraint
text:
Example: best response with a constraint
Maximize \(f(x)=2x-x^2\) subject to \(x\ge 0\).
Write the constraint as \(g(x)=-x\le 0\). Lagrangian:
\[
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)= (2x-x^2)-\lambda(-x)=2x-x^2+\lambda x.
\]
KKT: - Stationarity: \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=2-2x+\lambda=0\) - Primal feasibility: \(x\ge 0\) - Dual feasibility: \(\lambda\ge 0\) - Complementary slackness: \(\lambda x=0\)
From stationarity: \(2-2x+\lambda=0 \Rightarrow x=1+\lambda/2\).
If \(x>0\), then complementary slackness implies \(\lambda=0\), so \(x=1\). Check feasibility: \(1\ge 0\) yes. So the solution is \(x^*=1\).
(If the unconstrained maximizer had been negative, the constraint would bind and you’d get \(x^*=0\) with \(\lambda>0\).)

title: Dynamic reasoning
text:
In finite game trees with perfect information, backward induction solves from the end:

decide optimal actions at the last decision nodes

replace subgames by their continuation payoffs

move backward to the start

Intuition. Future choices discipline earlier choices.

title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
text:
A Bayesian game has private information (types). A Bayesian Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where each type best-responds given beliefs about others’ types.
Formally, each player \(i\) has type \(\theta_i\) and chooses an action via a strategy \(s_i(\theta_i)\). A BNE satisfies, for each type \(\theta_i\): \[
s_i(\theta_i)\in \arg\max_{a_i} \mathbb{E}\left[u_i(a_i, s_{-i}(\theta_{-i}), \theta_i,\theta_{-i})\mid \theta_i\right].
\]

title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
text:
A Bayesian game has private information (types). A Bayesian Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where each type best-responds given beliefs about others’ types.
Formally, each player \(i\) has type \(\theta_i\) and chooses an action via a strategy \(s_i(\theta_i)\). A BNE satisfies, for each type \(\theta_i\): \[
s_i(\theta_i)\in \arg\max_{a_i} \mathbb{E}\left[u_i(a_i, s_{-i}(\theta_{-i}), \theta_i,\theta_{-i})\mid \theta_i\right].
\]

title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
text:
Where it shows up

Static games of incomplete information (entry games, pricing with private costs)
Auctions (many auction models are BNE)
As the static benchmark for dynamic incomplete-information models

title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

List types and prior beliefs.
Write strategies as functions of types: \(a_i=s_i(\theta_i)\).
Compute each type’s expected payoff from each action.
Choose best responses by type.
Verify mutual best responses given beliefs.

title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
text:
Solved example (type-dependent best response)

Problem (context + question)
An investor chooses whether to fund a startup: \(F\) (fund) or \(R\) (reject).
The startup’s type is \(\theta\in\{S,W\}\) (strong or weak), with prior \(\Pr(S)=p\). If the investor funds: - payoff is \(+1\) if \(\theta=S\), - payoff is \(-1\) if \(\theta=W\).
If the investor rejects, payoff is \(0\).
Question: Find the investor’s optimal action as a function of \(p\) (a BNE decision rule).


Solution
Compute expected payoff from funding: \[
\mathbb{E}[\pi(F)] = p(1) + (1-p)(-1) = 2p-1.
\]
Rejecting yields: \[
\mathbb{E}[\pi(R)] = 0.
\]
So the investor funds iff \(2p-1\ge 0\), i.e. \[
p \ge \tfrac12.
\]
Result: Optimal strategy is: - choose \(F\) if \(p\ge 1/2\), - choose \(R\) if \(p<1/2\), - indifferent at \(p=1/2\).


Check
Given beliefs (the prior), the chosen action maximizes expected payoff.


Takeaway
BNE decisions are often threshold rules: act if expected benefit given beliefs is large enough.

title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
text:
Later-on analysis

If a signal is observed before acting, beliefs update via Bayes’ rule and the threshold shifts.
If the informed party can strategically choose information, you move toward signaling or cheap talk → PBE.
With many types/actions, equilibrium often has cutoff strategies and monotonicity structure.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
A trembling-hand perfect equilibrium (perfect equilibrium) is a Nash equilibrium that remains optimal when every player might make tiny mistakes (“trembles”).
Formally (intuition-level): a strategy profile is perfect if it is the limit of a sequence of fully mixed strategy profiles (every action played with positive probability) where each player’s strategy is a best response to the others in that sequence.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
A trembling-hand perfect equilibrium (perfect equilibrium) is a Nash equilibrium that remains optimal when every player might make tiny mistakes (“trembles”).
Formally (intuition-level): a strategy profile is perfect if it is the limit of a sequence of fully mixed strategy profiles (every action played with positive probability) where each player’s strategy is a best response to the others in that sequence.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games where Nash equilibria include weakly dominated or non-robust behavior
Refinement arguments: “Would this equilibrium survive small mistakes?”
Often discussed alongside proper equilibrium and sequential equilibrium

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
Why it exists (intuition)
If an equilibrium relies on assigning zero probability to “unlikely” actions, trembles force you to confront those actions. Strategies that are only optimal because some opponent action is assumed impossible may fail perfection.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Find Nash equilibria.
Check whether an equilibrium uses weakly dominated strategies or fragile best responses.
Consider small trembles: assume each player plays every action with tiny probability.
Ask: is the equilibrium strategy still a best response when opponents sometimes tremble?
If yes (as a limit), it’s perfect.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
section: Solved example (eliminating a weakly dominated equilibrium)
text:
Solved example (eliminating a weakly dominated equilibrium)

Problem (context + question)
Consider this 2×2 game (payoffs shown as (player 1, player 2)):
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& L & R\\ \hline
U & (1,1) & (0,1)\\
D & (1,0) & (0,0)
\end{array}
\]
Question: (i) Find all Nash equilibria. (ii) Which are trembling-hand perfect?


Solution
Step 1: Best responses - Player 1: - If player 2 plays \(L\): payoff from \(U\) is 1, from \(D\) is 1 → both \(U\) and \(D\) are best responses. - If player 2 plays \(R\): payoff from \(U\) is 0, from \(D\) is 0 → both are best responses. - Player 2: - If player 1 plays \(U\): payoffs are 1 from \(L\) and 1 from \(R\) → both best responses. - If player 1 plays \(D\): payoffs are 0 from \(L\) and 0 from \(R\) → both best responses.
So every pure profile is a Nash equilibrium (players are indifferent everywhere).
Step 2: Add trembles Suppose player 2 trembles: plays \(L\) with probability \(1-\varepsilon\) and \(R\) with probability \(\varepsilon>0\).
Player 1’s expected payoff from: - \(U\): \((1-\varepsilon)\cdot 1 + \varepsilon\cdot 0 = 1-\varepsilon\) - \(D\): \((1-\varepsilon)\cdot 1 + \varepsilon\cdot 0 = 1-\varepsilon\)
Still indifferent. So trembles do not break player 1’s indifference.
Now suppose player 1 trembles: plays \(U\) with probability \(1-\delta\) and \(D\) with probability \(\delta>0\).
Player 2’s expected payoff from: - \(L\): \((1-\delta)\cdot 1 + \delta\cdot 0 = 1-\delta\) - \(R\): \((1-\delta)\cdot 1 + \delta\cdot 0 = 1-\delta\)
Still indifferent.
Result: In this particular game, trembles do not select: equilibria are robust because payoffs create genuine indifference.


Takeaway
Perfection rules out equilibria that only work by assuming “impossible” actions never happen. But if the game truly makes players indifferent, perfection won’t refine further.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
Later-on analysis

Proper equilibrium strengthens perfection by making “worse mistakes” exponentially less likely.
In extensive-form games, sequential equilibrium is the tremble-based refinement with beliefs.
In many applied models, perfection is used to exclude equilibria involving weakly dominated actions.

Cheap talk baseline → Babbling equilibrium always exists

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Nash equilibrium (NE)

Pure NE

(Optional) Remove strictly dominated actions.
Compute best responses.
Intersections of best responses = pure NE.



Mixed NE (quick 2×2 method)
Let player 1 mix \(p\) on \(U\) (and \(1-p\) on \(D\)). Let player 2 mix \(q\) on \(L\) (and \(1-q\) on \(R\)). 1) Make player 1 indifferent between \(U\) and \(D\) → solve for \(q\). 2) Make player 2 indifferent between \(L\) and \(R\) → solve for \(p\). 3) Check \(p,q\in[0,1]\) and supports are consistent.
Common pitfall: mixing is only required when the opponent is indifferent among the actions in their support.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)

Backward induction (finite perfect-information trees)

Start at the last decision nodes.
Choose optimal action there.
Replace that subgame with its continuation payoff.
Move backward until the root.

Common pitfall: using non-credible threats (actions that wouldn’t be optimal if reached).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)

Write types and prior \(\Pr(\theta)\).
Strategy is type-contingent: \(a_i=s_i(\theta_i)\).
For each type, compute expected payoff for each action.
Choose best responses for each type; verify consistency across players.

Common pitfall: forgetting strategies are functions of type, not single actions.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
A PBE is (strategies, beliefs) satisfying: - Sequential rationality: actions optimal at every information set. - Bayes consistency on-path: update beliefs using Bayes’ rule where possible.

Standard workflow (signaling/screening)

Guess form: separating / pooling / semi-separating.
Propose strategies for sender types + receiver actions.
Compute on-path posteriors via Bayes.
Check receiver best responses given beliefs.
Check each sender type’s incentive constraints (no profitable deviations).
Specify off-path beliefs (carefully) and re-check deviations.

Common pitfall: not stating off-path beliefs, or using off-path beliefs that “magically” punish deviations without justification (sequential equilibrium addresses this).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Sequential equilibrium (SE)
Sequential equilibrium is PBE + a discipline on beliefs: - Beliefs must be limits of Bayes-updated beliefs from fully mixed trembles.

Practical use
If your PBE relies heavily on off-path beliefs: 1) Add tiny tremble probabilities to every action. 2) Compute implied posteriors. 3) Take limits → see which beliefs are justifiable. 4) Re-check optimality.
Common pitfall: treating off-path beliefs as completely free.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)

Receiver ignores message: same action after every message.
Beliefs stay at the prior (or any belief consistent with ignoring).
Sender is indifferent over messages because messages don’t affect actions.

Use: baseline; compare informative equilibria against it.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium

Start from a Nash equilibrium.
Ask whether it survives when opponents sometimes make small mistakes.
Equilibria relying on “impossible” actions not happening can fail.

Heuristic: if an equilibrium uses weakly dominated actions or fragile indifference, perfection may eliminate it.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Proper equilibrium
Like perfect equilibrium, but: - very bad mistakes are much less likely than slightly bad mistakes.
Use: sharper selection when perfection is not selective enough.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Correlated equilibrium (CE)

Specify a distribution over action profiles (recommendations).
For each player and each recommendation, write obedience constraints: following ≥ deviating.
If all constraints hold, it’s a CE.

Memory aid: “Follow the recommendation because conditional on it, deviating doesn’t help.”

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Rationalizability

Iteratively delete strictly dominated actions.
Repeat in the reduced game until no more deletions.
Remaining actions are rationalizable.

Common pitfall: weak dominance deletion can be order-dependent (start with strict).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Mini glossary (quick)

NE: best response to best response.
SPE: NE in every subgame (credible).
BNE: NE with types; best response in expectation.
PBE: strategies + beliefs; Bayes on-path; sequentially rational.
SE: PBE + tremble-consistent beliefs.
CE: equilibrium over distributions; “obey the signal.”
Rationalizability: what survives iterated strict dominance.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
In cheap talk, messages are costless and non-binding. A babbling equilibrium is one in which messages convey no information: the receiver’s action does not depend on the message, and the sender is indifferent across messages.
Babbling equilibria exist very generally and serve as a baseline.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
In cheap talk, messages are costless and non-binding. A babbling equilibrium is one in which messages convey no information: the receiver’s action does not depend on the message, and the sender is indifferent across messages.
Babbling equilibria exist very generally and serve as a baseline.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
Where it shows up

Cheap talk models (sender–receiver)
Communication settings with strong preference misalignment
As the “uninformative” benchmark when discussing informative equilibria (partition, separating)

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Make the receiver ignore messages: choose the same action after any message.
Set receiver beliefs equal to the prior (or any belief consistent with ignoring messages).
Verify receiver optimality under those beliefs.
Verify sender indifference: since messages don’t affect actions, any message is optimal.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
Solved example (fully worked)

Problem (context + question)
A sender observes \(\theta\in\{0,1\}\) with prior \(\Pr(\theta=1)=1/2\). Sender sends costless message \(m\in\{\text{low},\text{high}\}\). Receiver chooses action \(a\in\{0,1\}\).
Receiver payoff: \[
u_R(a,\theta)=\mathbf{1}\{a=\theta\}.
\]
Sender payoff (biased toward \(a=1\)): \[
u_S(a,\theta)=\mathbf{1}\{a=1\}.
\]
Question: Exhibit a babbling equilibrium (strategies + beliefs) and verify it.


Solution
A babbling equilibrium has receiver ignore the message.
Step 1 (receiver best response when ignoring messages): Under the prior, \(\Pr(\theta=1)=1/2\). Then - payoff from \(a=1\) is \(1/2\), - payoff from \(a=0\) is \(1/2\).
Receiver is indifferent, so a valid best response is: \[
a=0 \quad \text{after both messages}.
\]
Step 2 (sender incentives): If the receiver always plays \(a=0\), sender payoff is always \(0\) regardless of message. So the sender is indifferent and can send any message.
Let sender strategy be: always send “high”.
Step 3 (beliefs): Receiver beliefs do not depend on the message (since messages are ignored). Keep the prior: \[
\Pr(\theta=1\mid m)=1/2 \quad \text{for both } m\in\{\text{low},\text{high}\}.
\]
Result (babbling equilibrium): - Sender: always send “high”. - Receiver: always choose \(a=0\). - Beliefs: posterior equals prior after any message.


Check

Receiver optimality: given prior, \(a=0\) is a best response (ties).
Sender optimality: given receiver ignores messages, any message is optimal.
Beliefs are consistent with the equilibrium (receiver does not condition on \(m\)).



Takeaway
Babbling equilibria always exist because cheap messages can be ignored.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
Later-on analysis

Informative equilibria require structure: partial alignment, restrictions on message space, or repeated interaction.
Adding costs converts cheap talk into signaling, where credibility can be restored.
Many refinements aim to rule out “unreasonable” beliefs or equilibria, but babbling is a genuine equilibrium prediction in many environments.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
A Perfect Bayesian equilibrium is a pair (strategies, beliefs) in a dynamic game with incomplete information such that:

Sequential rationality: at every information set, each player’s action is optimal given their beliefs and others’ strategies.
Belief consistency (Bayes on-path): beliefs are updated using Bayes’ rule wherever possible along the equilibrium path.

Off-path (zero-probability) histories require beliefs to be specified; this can create multiple PBEs.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
A Perfect Bayesian equilibrium is a pair (strategies, beliefs) in a dynamic game with incomplete information such that:

Sequential rationality: at every information set, each player’s action is optimal given their beliefs and others’ strategies.
Belief consistency (Bayes on-path): beliefs are updated using Bayes’ rule wherever possible along the equilibrium path.

Off-path (zero-probability) histories require beliefs to be specified; this can create multiple PBEs.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
Where it shows up

Signaling games (education, quality signals)
Screening models with dynamic interaction
Any extensive-form game with imperfect information

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Guess an equilibrium form (separating / pooling / semi-separating).
Specify strategies for all players.
Derive beliefs using Bayes’ rule on-path.
Check sequential rationality at every information set:

receiver best-responds given beliefs,
sender type best-responds given receiver strategy.

Specify off-path beliefs and verify no profitable deviations.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
section: Solved example (pooling PBE in a signaling game)
text:
Solved example (pooling PBE in a signaling game)

Problem (context + question)
Types: worker \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\) with \(\Pr(H)=p\).
Worker chooses education \(e\in\{0,1\}\). Employer observes \(e\) and offers wage \(w\in\{w_H,w_L\}\).
Productivity: - If type \(H\): output value is \(2\) - If type \(L\): output value is \(1\)
Employer is competitive and pays expected productivity given beliefs: - pay \(w_H=2\) if believes \(H\) for sure, - pay \(w_L=1\) if believes \(L\) for sure, - pay \(w=p\cdot 2+(1-p)\cdot 1 = 1+p\) if belief is \(\Pr(H)=p\).
Education costs: - \(c_H(1)=0.2\), \(c_L(1)=0.8\), and \(c_H(0)=c_L(0)=0\).
Question: Construct a pooling PBE where both types choose \(e=0\).


Solution
We propose a pooling strategy: - Worker: \(e(\theta)=0\) for both \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\). - Employer: after observing \(e=0\), pay \(w(0)=1+p\) (belief equals prior); after \(e=1\), specify an off-path belief.
Step 1 (beliefs on-path): Since both types choose \(e=0\), observing \(e=0\) yields posterior \(\Pr(H\mid e=0)=p\). So paying \(w(0)=1+p\) is consistent.
Step 2 (employer sequential rationality): Given belief \(p\) after \(e=0\), competitive wage is \(1+p\). Good.
Now choose an off-path belief after \(e=1\). Let employer believe \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)=0\) (i.e., “only low types deviate”), so employer pays \(w(1)=1\).
Step 3 (worker incentive constraints): - Type \(H\) payoff if follow pooling (\(e=0\)): \(1+p\). If deviate to \(e=1\): wage \(1\) minus cost \(0.2\) → \(1-0.2=0.8\). So \(H\) does not deviate if \(1+p \ge 0.8\), which holds for all \(p\in[0,1]\).

Type \(L\) payoff if follow pooling: \(1+p\). If deviate to \(e=1\): wage \(1\) minus cost \(0.8\) → \(0.2\). So \(L\) never deviates.

Result (pooling PBE): - Worker: both types choose \(e=0\). - Employer beliefs: \(\Pr(H\mid e=0)=p\); off-path set \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)=0\). - Employer wages: \(w(0)=1+p\), \(w(1)=1\).


Check

Beliefs on-path follow Bayes’ rule.
Actions are optimal at each information set given beliefs. So it is a PBE.



Takeaway
PBE requires beliefs; off-path beliefs can support pooling by punishing deviations.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
Later-on analysis

Pooling PBEs can be fragile: refinements (sequential equilibrium, intuitive criterion) restrict off-path beliefs.
Separating PBEs require incentive compatibility inequalities (high type willing to signal; low type not).
PBE is a practical workhorse; just be explicit about beliefs and on/off-path behavior.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
A subgame perfect equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium of an extensive-form game that induces a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
Intuition: strategies must be credible not only along the equilibrium path but also after any possible history.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
A subgame perfect equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium of an extensive-form game that induces a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
Intuition: strategies must be credible not only along the equilibrium path but also after any possible history.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
Where it shows up

Extensive-form games with perfect information (classic backward induction)
Dynamic games where credibility of threats/promises matters
Bargaining models (alternating offers) are solved using SPE

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Identify subgames (in perfect-information games, every decision node typically starts a subgame).
Solve the last subgames first (optimize at terminal decision nodes).
Replace each solved subgame by its continuation payoff.
Continue backward until the start: this is backward induction.
The resulting strategy profile is an SPE (in finite perfect-information games).

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
Solved example (backward induction)

Problem (context + question)
A landlord (player 1) offers a rent increase: \(L\) (low) or \(H\) (high). The tenant (player 2) observes and chooses accept \(A\) or move \(M\).
Payoffs: - \((L,A)=(2,2)\), \((L,M)=(0,1)\) - \((H,A)=(3,0)\), \((H,M)=(0,1)\)
Question: Find the SPE.


Solution
Step 1 (solve tenant’s decision in each subgame): - After \(L\): tenant compares payoff \(2\) (accept) vs \(1\) (move) → chooses \(A\). - After \(H\): tenant compares payoff \(0\) (accept) vs \(1\) (move) → chooses \(M\).
So tenant strategy is: after \(L\) play \(A\), after \(H\) play \(M\).
Step 2 (landlord anticipates tenant’s response): - If landlord chooses \(L\), outcome is \((2,2)\). - If landlord chooses \(H\), tenant moves, outcome is \((0,1)\).
Landlord prefers \(L\) because \(2>0\).
Result (SPE): - Landlord plays \(L\). - Tenant plays \(A\) after \(L\) and \(M\) after \(H\). - Outcome: \((L,A)\).


Check

Tenant’s actions are optimal in each subgame.
Given tenant’s strategy, landlord’s choice is optimal at the start. So the strategy profile is Nash in every subgame.



Takeaway
SPE rules out non-credible threats by requiring optimal behavior after every history.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
Later-on analysis

With imperfect information, “subgame” may not be well-defined → PBE / sequential equilibrium.
With multiple SPE, equilibrium selection becomes a separate question.
In repeated games, SPE sets are large; punishments must still be credible.

title: Repeated games
text: A repeated game plays the same stage game over time (finitely or infinitely many periods). Strategies can condition on history.

title: Repeated games
text: A repeated game plays the same stage game over time (finitely or infinitely many periods). Strategies can condition on history.

title: Repeated games
text:
What’s special

Past behavior can be rewarded/punished → enables cooperation even when the one-shot game would not.
Central ideas: incentives over time, credibility, and equilibrium path vs off-path threats.
Infinite-horizon models often use a discount factor \(\delta\in(0,1)\).

title: Repeated games
section: One example (grim trigger in repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma)
text:
One example (grim trigger in repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma)
Stage game: cooperate \(C\) or defect \(D\). Typical payoffs: - \((C,C)\) gives \((R,R)\), - \((D,C)\) gives \((T,S)\), - \((C,D)\) gives \((S,T)\), - \((D,D)\) gives \((P,P)\), with \(T>R>P>S\).
Grim trigger strategy: start with \(C\), continue \(C\) unless someone defects; after any defection, play \(D\) forever.
Incentive condition (intuition): cooperate today if the present temptation \(T-R\) is outweighed by the discounted future loss from punishment. Cooperation can be sustained if \(\delta\) is sufficiently high.

title: Repeated games
text:
Story
Two graduate students, Kai and Mira, share an office. Each week they decide whether to clean the shared space. Cleaning is effortful; skipping is tempting. If one keeps cleaning while the other skips, resentment builds. If both skip, the office becomes miserable.
Because the choice repeats, today’s action can trigger tomorrow’s response.

title: Repeated games
text:
Model

Stage actions: \(C\) (clean), \(S\) (shirk)
Stage payoffs (toy): PD-like
Infinite horizon with discount factor \(\delta\in(0,1)\)
Strategies can condition on history

title: Repeated games
text:
Equilibrium (cooperation via grim trigger)
Grim trigger: play \(C\) unless someone shirks; after any shirking, play \(S\) forever.
Compare deviating once vs cooperating on-path (player 1, symmetric): - Cooperate forever payoff: \(\frac{2}{1-\delta}\) - Deviate once (get 3 now, then punished with 1 forever): \(3 + \frac{\delta}{1-\delta}\)
Cooperation is sustainable if: \[
\frac{2}{1-\delta} \ge 3+\frac{\delta}{1-\delta}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\delta \ge \frac12.
\]

title: Repeated games
text:
Later-on analysis

Finite horizon: backward induction kills cooperation near the end (unless there are other frictions).
Noisy actions: if mistakes happen, harsh punishments can be inefficient; “forgiving” strategies (tit-for-tat variants) become relevant.
Multiple equilibria: repeated games often admit many equilibrium paths; selection becomes a real question.

title: Auctions
text: Auctions allocate an item based on bids. Models differ by: - format (first-price, second-price, English, Dutch), - values (private values vs common values), - information (signals, asymmetries).

title: Auctions
text: Auctions allocate an item based on bids. Models differ by: - format (first-price, second-price, English, Dutch), - values (private values vs common values), - information (signals, asymmetries).

title: Auctions
text:
What’s special

Bidding strategies trade off winning probability vs payment.
In private values with risk-neutral bidders, many formats have linked outcomes (revenue equivalence under conditions).
In common-value settings, bidders fear the winner’s curse.

title: Auctions
text:
One example (second-price auction, private values)
Each bidder has value \(v_i\) for the item. In a second-price (Vickrey) auction, the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid.
A dominant strategy is: \[
b_i = v_i.
\]
Intuition: your bid only affects whether you win, not what you pay conditional on winning. Overbidding risks winning at a price above your value; underbidding risks losing when you would have profited.

title: Auctions
text:
Story
A tutor releases one Saturday slot. Many students bid; each has private urgency. The rule for who pays what shapes bidding incentives.

title: Auctions
text:
Model

Bidders \(i=1,\dots,n\)
Private values \(v_i\)
Bids \(b_i\)
Auction format determines allocation and payment

title: Auctions
text:
Equilibrium (second-price auction)
In a second-price auction, the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid. A dominant strategy is: \[
b_i=v_i.
\]
Reason (one-line): your bid affects winning, but the price conditional on winning is the opponent’s bid, not yours.

title: Auctions
text:
Later-on analysis

First-price auctions: equilibrium involves bid shading; risk aversion matters.
Common values: winner’s curse and information aggregation dominate.
Reserve prices and optimal design: mechanism design connects auctions to revenue maximization.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
A normal-form game models simultaneous choice: players pick actions without observing others’ choices.
A finite two-player game is often represented by payoff matrices \((A,B)\).

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
A normal-form game models simultaneous choice: players pick actions without observing others’ choices.
A finite two-player game is often represented by payoff matrices \((A,B)\).

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
What’s special

Strategies are complete plans chosen at once (pure or mixed).
Main solution concept: Nash equilibrium (possibly mixed).
Workhorse tools: best responses, dominance, indifference.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
One example (Prisoner’s Dilemma)
Actions: \(C\) (cooperate) or \(D\) (defect).
Payoffs: - \((C,C)=(2,2)\) - \((D,C)=(3,0)\) - \((C,D)=(0,3)\) - \((D,D)=(1,1)\)
Solution sketch. \(D\) strictly dominates \(C\) for each player, so the unique Nash equilibrium is \((D,D)\), even though \((C,C)\) is Pareto-better.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Story
Two independent cafés, North Bean and South Bean, sit across the same narrow street by a commuter station. Tomorrow morning there will be a marathon: heavy demand, impatient customers, and intense competition for foot traffic. Tonight, each café must decide whether to run a deep discount.
If only one café discounts, it steals attention and most walk-ins. If both discount, they split the crowd but both suffer thin margins. If neither discounts, both do fine—yet each fears being the only one who doesn’t discount.
They decide simultaneously: no café observes the other’s choice before committing.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Model

Players: cafés \(1,2\)
Actions: \(D\) (discount), \(N\) (normal)
Timing: simultaneous
Payoffs: profits

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Payoffs (toy)
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& D & N\\ \hline
D & (1,1) & (3,0)\\
N & (0,3) & (2,2)
\end{array}
\]

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Equilibrium (Nash)
Best responses: - If the other chooses \(N\), your best response is \(D\) (you gain market share). - If the other chooses \(D\), your best response is \(D\) (you avoid being undercut).
So \(D\) is a best response to both opponent actions: the unique Nash equilibrium is \((D,D)\).

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Later-on analysis

Why it matters: this is the basic logic behind price wars and “race to the bottom” outcomes.
If repeated: repeated interaction can sustain \((N,N)\) via punishments (see Repeated games).
If asymmetric costs: one café might never discount, shifting equilibrium and welfare.
